1:1.t: But the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah is said to belong to that time when Uzziah, who is called by another name Azariah, trying to claim for himself a priesthood not lawful for him, was struck with leprosy on his forehead; of this earthquake we also read at the beginning of Amos: The words of Amos, who was among the shepherds of Tekoa, which he saw concerning Israel in the days of Uzziah king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash king of Israel, two years before the earthquake. In short, after this wicked king died, at whose impiety the whole earth was shaken, Isaiah saw the great vision which he wove into his book.

The prophet Amos, who follows Joel and is the third of the twelve prophets, is not the same man whom we read of as the father of the prophet Isaiah. For that one is written with the first and last letters of his name, aleph and sade, and is interpreted strong and robust; this one, however, with ain and samech, and is interpreted a people torn away; the middle letters, mem and uau, are common to both. But among us, who do not have so great a difference of vowel letters, and of the letter s, which among the Hebrews is threefold, both these and other names seem to be the same, which among the Hebrews are distinguished by the diversity of their letters and by their own peculiarities. […]

The words of Amos, who was among the herdsmen of Tekoa, which he saw concerning Israel. But the Seventy, intending I know not what, translated: The words of Amos, which came to be in Accarim of Tekoa, which he saw on behalf of Jerusalem. And it should be known that this prophet prophesied, not on behalf of Jerusalem, which is not found at all in the Hebrew, but concerning Israel, that is, the ten tribes, which are called Israel and were in Samaria. And indeed Aquila and Symmachus and Theodotion translated this likewise. The first, then, the prophet Hosea, speaks to the ten tribes, which are called Ephraim, Samaria, the house of Joseph and Israel. […]

1:2.t: And he said: The Lord will roar from Zion, and from Jerusalem he will give his voice. And the beautiful places of the shepherds have mourned, and the top of Carmel has been dried up. LXX: And he said: The Lord has spoken out from Zion, and from Jerusalem he has given his voice; and the pastures of the shepherds have mourned, and the top of Carmel has withered. It is natural that all craftsmen speak in the examples of their own craft, and that each one should bring forward likenesses from the pursuit in which he has spent his life: for example, he who is a sailor and a helmsman compares his sadness to a storm, calls a loss a shipwreck, names his enemies contrary winds; […]

1:3.t: You must slay the allurements to vice while they are still only thoughts and dash the little ones of the daughter of Babylon against the stones where the serpent can leave no trail. Be wary and lay claim to the Lord's promise: "Let them not have dominion over me: then shall I be upright and I shall be innocent from the great transgression." For elsewhere also the Scripture testifies, "I will visit the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation." That is to say, God will not punish us at once for our thoughts and resolves but will send retribution upon their offspring or upon the evil deeds and habits of sin, which arise out of the offspring. […]

Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Damascus, and for four, I will not turn him back, because they threshed Gilead with iron carts. LXX: And the Lord said: For three impieties of Damascus, and for four, I will not turn away from them, because they sawed with iron saws the women with child in Gilead. For the threshing sledges, which in Hebrew are called arsoth, and were translated by Theodotion iron wheels, which we have rendered iron carts, the Seventy translated iron saws. It is, moreover, a kind of cart which rolls on iron, toothed wheels underneath, so that, when the grain has been shaken out, it may crush the stubble on the threshing floors and break up the chaff into fodder for the beasts of burden, because of the scarcity of hay.

We have spoken briefly about the causes of the different translation; now let us pass on to the sense of what has been said. First the word of God is directed against Damascus, in which Hazael reigned, who, at the time when Amos was prophesying, was pressing hard upon Israel, that is, the ten tribes, so much so that, after Ahab king of Israel had been overcome at Ramoth-gilead, he slaughtered and crushed the whole region which was called Gilead, and which had fallen as an inheritance to the half-tribe of Manasseh, like threshing sledges threshing grain on the threshing floors. This the prophet Elisha speaks of more fully in the volume of Kings, where we read it written: And he stood with him, and was troubled until his face was flushed; and the man of God wept. […]

And what is said at the beginning: For three crimes of Damascus, and for four, I will not turn him back, and according to the Seventy: Shall I not turn away from him?, that is, from the people of Damascus, or Aram, that is, the Syrian, can have this sense according to the history: If he had persecuted my people once, or a second time, I would grant pardon; but now, since he has shown himself cruel a third and a fourth time, so that he crushed the captive multitude with iron carts, ought I not to chastise him with blows? Ought I not to turn the face of my clemency away from him? But according to tropology we can say this: the first sin is to have thought what is evil; the second, to have consented to perverse thoughts; […]

This is what the prophet also says: 'For three and four sins I will not turn her back, says the Lord.' And he says this eight times. Now Amos speaks this, that is: you thought, I pardoned: you did it, I pardoned: you did not do penance, I pardoned: were you obliged even to teach evils? This is what is said, For three and four sins I will not be angry with you, says the Lord.

1:4.t: And I will send fire into the house of Hazael, and it will devour the houses of Ben-hadad. And I will break the bar of Damascus, and I will destroy the inhabitant from the plain of the idol. LXX: And I will send forth fire into the house of Hazael, and it will devour the foundations of the son of Ader. And I will break the bars of Damascus, and I will destroy the inhabitants from the plain of ὢν. He gives us to understand that Hazael, in the reigns of Uzziah and Jeroboam, had already died in Syria, and that his son Ben-hadad had succeeded him in the kingdom, from whom afterwards all the kings of Aram, that is, of Syria and Damascus, held the name Ben-hadad. […]

But the Lord will send fire into the house of Hazael, which they themselves call Hazael, that is, vision of God; a fire to consume the wood and stubble in them, and to devour the foundations of the son of Ader. For we ought to speak according to the Seventy as well, lest we seem to have set them out to no purpose: Ader is interpreted εὐπρέπεια, which we can call comeliness, because all the discourse of the heretics, being elegant and well composed and having the beauty of worldly eloquence, deceives its hearers the more easily.

Again, where in the Hebrew there is Benadad, and it is a single name, the Seventy translated the sons of Ader, deceived by the likeness of the letters res and daleth. In that place too where we said, from the house of pleasure, which in Hebrew is mebbeth eden, and all translated it likewise, the Seventy translated from the men of Charran, taking daleth, the middle letter of the name, for res, and, according to their custom, putting the Greek chi before ain, the first Hebrew letter. Cyrene also, which in Hebrew is called cira, they translated ἐπήκλητον, that is, called or named, because of the likeness of the word, since carae can be said for calling, and they understood the proper name as a common noun.

1:5.t: And I will break, he says, the bars of Damascus, and I will destroy the inhabitant from the plain of the idol: that is, all the strength of the Syrians, who, as with a kind of cart and with bars, kept off the onsets of their adversaries. But the plain of the idol, which in Hebrew is called auen, and which both the Seventy and Theodotion rendered ὢν, Symmachus and the Fifth edition translated iniquity; Aquila ἀνωφελοῦς, that is, useless, to show the vain help of idols, since the people of Damascus is taken captive when the Assyrian comes. […]

And by the bars of Damascus, as it were very strong and very firm bolts, let those be understood who are equipped with the art of dialectic and with the arguments of the philosophers. For example: he is called the door who conceived and brought forth a false dogma, like Arius in Alexandria; its bars and its very firm bolts are Euticius and Eunomius, who try to strengthen it with syllogisms and enthymemes, or rather with sophisms and pseudomena and sorites, which were wickedly invented by others. And when the bars of Damascus have been crushed and broken, he will also destroy the inhabitants from the plain of ὢν, which is interpreted labour or pain. For all the heretics have tried with excessive labour and with the pain of seeking to find some order and consistency for their heresy. […]

1:6.t: Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Gaza, and for four, I will not turn him back, because he carried away a complete captivity, to shut it up in Idumea. And I will send fire into the wall of Gaza, and it will devour its houses; and I will destroy the inhabitant from Azotus, and him who holds the sceptre from Ashkelon, and I will turn my hand upon Ekron, and the remnant of the Philistines will perish, says the Lord. LXX: Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of Gaza, and for four, I will not turn away from them, because they led captive the captivity of Solomon, to shut it up in Idumea; […]

According to tropology it seems that it should be explained by us thus: Gaza, which in Hebrew is called Aza, means strength or dominion; Solomon, peaceful; the Idumean, bloodthirsty and earthly; Azotus, that is, Esdod, fire of the breast, or of the paternal uncle, although some, wrongly reading dor for dod, think it means fire of generation; Ashkelon is interpreted murderous fire, or hung up and weighed; Ekron, στείρωσις, that is, barrenness, and ἐκρίζωσις, which is interpreted uprooting. Gaza, therefore, which promises itself the strength and dominion of its own knowledge, is accused of having shut up in Idumea captives from the household of Solomon. […]

1:7.t: Hence he says that he will send fire upon the walls and houses, or foundations, of Gaza, to devour and swallow up everything.

1:8.t: And because we read of five cities of the Philistines, which were struck with plagues on account of the wrong done to the ark, after Gaza he passes to Azotus, which is called Esdod, and again to Ashkelon, and with a terrible voice he threatens that he will destroy the inhabitants of Azotus, and him who holds the sceptre from Ashkelon, that is, the royal power, or the tribe of Ashkelon, so that no one may remain there, not even men of the last age, who support their trembling limbs with a guiding staff. And again he moves his hand to strike Ekron. […]

1:9.t: Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Tyre, and for four, I will not turn him back, because they shut up a perfect captivity in Idumea; and they did not remember the covenant of brothers, and I will send fire upon the wall of Tyre, and it shall devour its houses. LXX: Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of Tyre and for four I will not turn away from her, because they shut up the captivity of Solomon in Idumea, and they did not remember the testament of brothers. And I will send forth fire upon the walls of Tyre, and it shall devour its foundations. […]

Tyre means tribulation, or one who hems in; and every perverse doctrine strives to seize the truth, and to shut it up in earthly senses, and it did not remember the covenant of its brothers, that we ought to ascend from the letter to the spirit, from earthly things to heavenly ones; and that it is a precept for us to write out the sacred Scripture in our heart threefold. But God will send fire upon all the fortifications of Tyre, which will devour not only its walls but also its foundations. Concerning the captivity of Solomon, in place of which the Hebrew has consummate and perfect, we have spoken above.

1:10.t: Therefore he says that he will send fire upon its walls, and that it will devour its houses or foundations, which the prophet Ezekiel, in the vision of Tyre, records that Nebuchadnezzar king of the Chaldeans did, where he says: He will surround you with fortifications, and he will heap up a mound round about. And again: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon made his army serve a great service against Tyre. Every head was made bald, and every shoulder stripped of hair, and wages were not paid to him, nor to his army, for Tyre, for the service with which he served me against her, because his army heaped up a mound for taking Tyre, which formerly was an island. […]

1:11.t: Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Edom and for four I will not turn him back; because he pursued his brother with the sword, and violated his mercy, and held his fury beyond measure, and kept his indignation to the end; I will send fire into Teman, and it shall devour the houses of Bozrah. LXX: Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of Idumea and for four I will not turn away from them, because he pursued his brother with the sword, and violated the womb upon the earth, and seized his horror for a testimony, and kept his onset for ever; and I will send forth fire into Teman, and it shall devour the foundations of its walls. Edom is the same as Esau, so called because of the cooking of the red lentil, for the food of which he lost his birthright. […]

Whatever we have said about Esau and Jacob, let us refer to the Jews and the Christian people. For they, earthly and bloodthirsty, persecuted their brother Jacob, who supplanted them and took away their birthright, and they persecuted him with the sword, so that they confiscated the substance and possessions of the believers, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles; and they violated mercy and the rights of nature, and forgot their mother Rebekah, which means patience, who bore them together in Christ; and holding on to their ancient fury and wrath, to this day in their synagogues they blaspheme the Christian people under the name of Nazarenes, and provided only that they may kill us, they are willing to be burned with fire. […]

In all places the Scriptures call Esau cunning and crafty, and one who layeth up anger, and keepeth wrath, as it is said, "He keepeth his anger for ever, and he layeth up his wrath for ever and ever."
1:11.s: 13 Ascetic Discourses, Discourse 4 -- On Faith: First Discourse on Simplicity

1:12.t: Hence he threatens punishment for their crimes, and says: I will send fire into Teman, which is a region of the Idumeans, and it lies toward the southern quarter, which is what Teman means; this province is called not only Teman but also Daron and Nageb, because it faces the east wind and the south wind and the south-west wind. And as for what he says: It shall devour the houses of Bozrah, it signifies, not another city, as some think, but Idumea, ὀχυρωμένην and fortified, according to that which we read in Isaiah: Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah; this one beautiful in his robe, walking in the multitude of his strength?

1:13.t: Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of the sons of Ammon and for four I will not turn him back, because he ripped up the pregnant women of Gilead, to enlarge his border; and I will kindle fire on the wall of Rabbah, and it shall devour its houses with howling in the day of battle, and with a whirlwind in the day of commotion; and Melchom shall go into captivity, he and his princes together, says the Lord. LXX: Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of the sons of Ammon and for four I will not turn away from them, because he cut up the pregnant women of the Gileadites, that he might enlarge his borders; and I will kindle fire upon the walls of Rabbah, and it shall devour the foundations with shouting in the day of battle, and it shall be shaken in the day of its consummation; […]

Now between the cruelty of Damascus and that of the sons of Ammon there is this difference, that they crushed Gilead with iron carts, or the pregnant women of Gilead with iron saws; but these ripped up the pregnant women of Gilead, to enlarge their border. In the people of Damascus, who drink blood, are understood the heretics, who not only have broken the people of God away from the Church, but have also crushed them and ground them with iron teeth, of whom it is written: Who devour my people as a meal of bread? In the sons of Ammon, which means people of grief, or my people, we understand the schismatics, who do indeed separate a deceived multitude from the Church of God, and break off and divide untrained souls which have lately conceived the word of Christ; […]

The [false teachers] are also to be admonished to consider well, how sacred Scripture is set up as a kind of lantern for us in the night of this life. When the words are not rightly understood, darkness is the result. And obviously, their perverse mind would not hurry them into a false understanding unless they were first inflated with pride. For while they think themselves wiser than others, they scorn to follow others in matters which these understand better. What is more, in order that they may extort from the untutored crowd a reputation for knowledge, they make every endeavor to discredit what these rightly understand and to confirm their own perverse views. Therefore, it is well said by the prophet, "They have ripped up the women with child of Gilead to enlarge their border." […]

1:14.t: Hence he threatens that he will kindle fire on the walls of Rabbah, which was the metropolis of the Ammonites, so that its houses may be devoured amid the shouting and howling of the conquering army; in the day of commotion and of whirlwind, when, Nebuchadnezzar conquering, its captives will be led away, and the idol of the Ammonites, which is called Melchom, that is, their king, will be carried off to the Assyrians; and its princes, that is, its priests, will be led away together. Priests is not in the Hebrew, but princes. So the Seventy added priests, so that, if you wish to know who these princes are, you may hear: priests.

2:1.t: Now to prove that in the present place Moab is to be understood of the pride of the philosophers, of whom it is said: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the understanding of the understanding I will reject, a few examples from the prophet must be unfolded: Amos says: Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of Moab and for four I will not turn away from him, because he burned the bones of the king of Edom to ashes — for truly, whatever there is in the world of perverse doctrines, whatever pertains to earthly knowledge and is thought to be robust, this is overthrown by the dialectical art and, like a fire, dissolved into ashes and embers, so that what was thought to be strongest is proved to be worth nothing —; […]

Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Moab and for four I will not turn him back, because he burned the bones of the king of Idumea even to ashes. And I will send fire into Moab, and it shall devour the houses of Kerioth, and Moab shall die in the noise, in the blast of the trumpet, and I will destroy the judge from the midst of it, and I will slay all its princes with him, says the Lord. LXX: Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of Moab and for four I will not turn away from them, because he burned the bones of the king of Idumea into ashes; and I will send forth fire into Moab, and it shall devour the foundations of its cities, and Moab shall die in weakness with shouting, and with the voice of the trumpet; […]

But just as one ought not to carry off the perfect captivity, or that of Solomon, and shut it up in Idumea, so as to make lowly and earthly men out of lofty and heavenly ones, which Gaza and Tyre are recorded to have done, so we ought not to burn the bones of the king of Idumea and dissolve them into ashes and embers. The Jews transfer the spiritual understanding into Idumean flesh, and the royal sense, which is engaged in the letter, and is most solid and most firm, they enervate and break down with certain genealogies and superfluous traditions, and reduce to dust; and not only do they do this, but all the heretics, who would have God, after the manner of a human likeness, sit on a high and lofty throne and set his feet upon the earth, so that, of course, they may not dangle; […]

2:2.t: For this reason, therefore, they say, God declares that he will send fire into Moab, either the metropolis of the Moabites, from which the whole province was named, or the whole province, so that it might devour the houses of Kerioth, which is the name of a city; although the Seventy translated of its cities, that is, of Moab; and that it will perish in the noise and in the howling of the conquering army, of which the one is called in Hebrew saon, the other therua; and in the blast of the trumpet or horn, for this is what sophar signifies. And when Moab has perished, the counsel of its princes and judges will be vain, its cities and its leaders being overthrown alike.

And for that reason the Lord sends fire into Moab, which means from the father, because he was indeed born of God, but has abandoned him. And it will devour its cities, or towns, which is what Kerioth means. Hence also Kiriath-jearim is turned into our language as village of the forests. And Moab will die in no other way than in shouting, and noise, and howling, and the blast of the horn, so that they may be overwhelmed by the lofty senses which in the holy books are compared to the blasts of the horn. Then the divine word destroys both the judges and the princes, and all who preside over earthly works, and it commands the teachers of the Church: Go up onto a high mountain, you who bring good tidings to Zion; lift up your voice, you who preach to Jerusalem.

2:4.t: Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Judah, and for four I will not turn him back, because he has cast away the law of the Lord, and has not kept his commandments; for their idols have deceived them, after which their fathers had gone, and I will send fire into Judah and it shall devour the houses of Jerusalem. LXX: Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of the sons of Judah, and for four I will not turn away from them, because they have rejected the law of the Lord, and have not kept his precepts; and they have been deceived in their vanities, which their fathers followed, and I will send forth fire into Judah, and it shall devour the foundations of Jerusalem. […]

Whatever we have said about Judah is referred to the Church, in which there is the true confession, and the peace of the Lord, and the vision of truth. And in this it is reproved, that it has despised the law of God and has not done his commandments, and that each one, adoring his own vices and sins, has begun to have as God that by which he has been overcome, as the apostle Peter says: For by what one is overcome, of this he is also the slave. The miser worships gold, the glutton his belly, the lustful man his member and Baal-peor; the wanton woman, who, living in pleasures, is dead, adores venereal pleasures.

2:5.t: Hence the Lord threatens that he will send fire into Judah also, to devour the houses and the foundations of Jerusalem, not of that Jerusalem in which the vision of peace abides, but of those which have arisen in various cities under the name of Jerusalem.

Hence the Lord will send fire into Judah, and it will devour the most wicked houses and the vicious foundations, which have destroyed the glory of Jerusalem; and at the same time we learn that the Creator of all has care not only of Judah and Israel but of all the nations; and that, according to the Apostle, those who have sinned without the law perish without the law, and those who have committed offences under the law are judged by the law of the Lord.

2:6.t: Many, truly, are the shoes of the sinful soul, by which it is bound and cramped. For each man is cramped by the cords of his own sins. Accordingly, Abraham swears to the king of Sodom, "I will not take of all that is thine, from a thread to a shoe-latchet." On account of these being defiled and polluted on the earth, every kind of wrong and selfishness engrosses life. As the Lord reproves Israel by Amos, saying, "For three iniquities of Israel, yea, for four, I will not turn him back; because they have given away the righteous for silver, and the needy for a pair of shoes, which tread upon the dust of the ground."
2:6.s: Fragments Found in Greek Only in the Oxford Edition

2:6.t: He might also have been betrayed by any stranger, did I not find that even here too he fulfilled a psalm: "He who did eat bread with me has lifted up his heel against me." And without a price might he have been betrayed. For what need of a traitor was there in the case of one who offered himself to the people openly and might quite as easily have been captured by force as taken by treachery? This might, no doubt, have been well enough for another Christ but would not have been suitable in one who was accomplishing prophecies. For it was written, "The righteous one did they sell for silver." […]

Thus says the Lord: For three crimes of Israel, and for four I will not turn him back, because he sold the righteous for silver and the poor for sandals, they who crush the heads of the poor upon the dust of the earth and turn aside the way of the humble; and a son and his father went in to the girl, to profane my holy name; and upon garments taken in pledge they reclined beside every altar, and they drank the wine of the condemned in the house of their God. LXX: Thus says the Lord: For three impieties of Israel, and for four I will not turn away from them, because he sold the righteous for silver, and the poor for the sake of sandals, which tread upon the dust of the earth; […]

But we, who have shown in Hosea that under the name of Israel, and of Samaria, and of Ephraim, and of the sons of Joseph — of which tribe was Jeroboam, who separated the people from the kingdom of David and from Jerusalem and from the temple of God — the heretics are signified, let us understand now too, after Judah and Jerusalem, which is interpreted as the Church, that the prophetic discourse is directed at the heretics, who sell a holy and righteous man, and a poor one too, for money. The poor and righteous man is the churchman who does not have knowledge of the Scriptures, but, content with simplicity, does the commandments that have been enjoined, of whom it is written: The poor man does not endure threatening. And to the Galatians: Only that we should be mindful of the poor. […]

He does not leave him unpunished, but rather subjects to punishments Israel, that is, the tribes in Samaria. And that they themselves, sinning unguardedly, have all but consumed the tranquility owed by God to the weak, the turning away for three and four sins would show, which having suffered they must necessarily be subjected to terrible things, and be in every evil. Therefore, the divine David, fearing this thing, and knowing it to be a cause of destruction, implored, saying, "Do not turn Your face from me, and do not turn away in wrath from Your servant." For wrath always follows, and, as it were, accompanies the turnings away.

"They sell the righteous for silver, and the needy for a pair of sandals": They did not endure to speak rightly and justly, and to render for each of those being judged the justice that accords with the law. But if it happened that a man was righteous, sober and gentle, modest and unboastful; for such a one would be understood as both righteous and needy, or poor in spirit; being brought to judgment by one of the more powerful, this man is sold to his enemies, although the law clearly proclaimed, "You shall not take person in judgment;" and again, "You shall not slay the innocent and the just." For the one entrusted with judging is certainly established in the order of God, to whom alone judging is proper. "For there is one lawgiver and judge," according to the voice of the saint. […]

2:7.t: How then is it that while forbidding the greater he was silent about the less? Because the example of the patriarch seemed injurious to many who indulged their flesh so far as to live with sisters in their life time. What ought to be my course? To quote the Scriptures, or to work out what they leave unsaid? In these laws it is not written that a father and son ought not to have the same concubine, but, in the prophet, it is thought deserving of the most extreme condemnation, “A man and his father” it is said “will go in unto the same maid.” […]

These, according to the Seventy, strike the poor man on the head; according to the Hebrew, they crush the heads of the poor upon the dust of the earth, and they are lifted up into such pride that they are unwilling to walk with the humble. And lest this misdeed be thought small, a son and his father went in to one girl, to violate the holy name of God. Whatever, therefore, is done shamefully is referred to an injury against God, who says: Through you my name is blasphemed among the nations. This is what the Apostle also writes to the Corinthians: It is actually reported that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not even among the nations, so that someone has his father's wife. […]

And the heretics strike the heads of the poor, although this is not read in the Hebrew, because they have turned aside the way of the humble. The way of the humble is that which says: I am the way, and the life, and the truth, which calls us to walk along it, and says: Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. But all the chiefs of the heretics swell with pride, of whom the Apostle also speaks: Lest, being puffed up, he fall into the judgment of the devil; who says: I will ascend into heaven, above the stars of heaven I will set my nest, I will be like the Most High. Hence the proud heretics God resists, but to the humble churchmen he gives grace. The son and the father, too, went in to one girl, to violate and profane the holy name of God. […]

2:8.t: And because every outrage, once it has passed the boundary of shame, adds crimes to crimes and always advances to worse things, the ten tribes even reclined upon garments taken in pledge beside every altar, which the Hebrews interpret thus: upon the garments of those who were unwilling to go to the idols, which they had extorted by force, they reclined, feasting in the idol's temple. But according to the Seventy, so great was their contempt for God that they stretched out with cords beside the altar their garments in which they sleep, or in which they commit fornication, and made παραπετάσματα, that is, coverings, so that no one could see them committing fornication in the temple; […]

But also, binding their garments with cords, they make coverings beside the altar, holding out the faith of Christ as a screen. For as many as have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ, and they set their garments, which they have bound with the cords of sins, before the eyes of those who look, so that their outrages may not be seen, and so that whoever looks at the altar may not suspect the debauchery. This all the heretics do, committing fornication under the Christian name, and spreading the testimonies of the Scriptures over their errors and lies as a screen. Hence the apostles too spread their garments on the foal of the ass, so that the Lord might sit more softly, and might mount the road paved from the law and the prophets. […]

2:9.t: Therefore, before God led us out of the land of Egypt, out of the iron furnace, he destroyed before our face the Amorite, who is called bitter, or λαλητὸς, that is, speaking, or famous and celebrated in frequent talk. Now this Amorite and king of the Amorites is called Sihon, an unfruitful and barren tree, not because it bears no fruit, but because it brings forth bad fruit, of which it is said: Every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and cast into the fire. And of the false prophets we read: Who come in the clothing of sheep, and inwardly are ravening wolves; by their fruits you will know them, by their bad fruits, that is. Whether, then, it bears no fruit, or bears fruit but not good fruit, it is called an unfruitful tree. […]

But I destroyed the Amorite from before their face, whose height was the height of the cedars, and he was strong as an oak; and I crushed his fruit above, and his roots beneath. It is I who made you go up from the land of Egypt, and I led you out in the desert forty years, that you might possess the land of the Amorite; and I raised up of your sons for prophets, and of your young men Nazirites. LXX: But I took away the Amorite from before their face, whose loftiness was as the height of the cedar, and he was strong as an oak; and I dried up his fruit above, and his roots below. I led you out of the land of Egypt, and led you around in the desert forty years, that you might possess the land of the Amorites; […]

His roots too he cut down and broke in pieces, so that nothing of the evil tree might sprout afterwards; and the Lord himself made us go out from the world and, through forty years, a number which always belongs to affliction and fasting, to mourning and sorrow, come through tribulations and straits to the holy land, that we might first possess the land of the Amorite, and the region that was once his might become our possession; and that afterwards he might raise up prophets from our sons, all the holy men who received the prophetic spirit, of whom we read more fully in the first epistle to the Corinthians; […]

2:11.t:
Is it not so, sons of Israel, says the Lord.

And you will give the Nazirites wine to drink, and you were commanding the prophets, saying: Do not prophesy. LXX: likewise. While I was bestowing such great benefits on you, so as to kill your adversaries and hand their land over to you, and to choose prophets and Nazirites from your sons and young men and consecrate them to my worship. Can you say that I did not do these things, and deny my clemency toward you, through which you live?

2:12.t: Samson and Samuel drank neither wine nor strong drink, for they were children of promise and conceived in abstinence and fasting. Aaron and the other priests when about to enter the temple refrained from all intoxicating drink for fear they should die. From this we learn that they die who minister in the church without sobriety. And hence it is a reproach against Israel: "You gave my Nazirites wine to drink."

You who broke out into such madness that you made my Nazirites drunk with wine, though they are commanded by the law not to drink anything that can intoxicate, and charged the prophets not to prophesy in my name. This is what Amaziah the priest of Bethel also commanded the prophet Amos, whom we now have in hand; and Jeremiah was ordered by the king not to speak the words of the Lord to the people, to such a degree that the king even burned his discourses in the fire. From this passage Tatian, the chief of the Encratites, tries to build up his heresy, asserting that wine must not be drunk, since it is commanded in the law that the Nazirites should not drink wine, and now those who give the Nazirites wine to drink are accused by the prophet. […]

2:13.t: But now let us return to our own. God threatens that he will roll a cart weighed down with hay or stubble beneath them, so that, since they have no grain to be stored up in barns, their hay and stubble may be burned up in the fire. This is the hay of which the prophet says: Let them become like the hay of the buildings, which withers before it is plucked up. And: All flesh is hay. And the stubble is that over whose burning the prophet laments so mournfully, saying: Woe is me. For I have become like one who gathers stubble in the harvest, and like grapes at the vintage, when there is no cluster to eat, the first-ripe. Woe is me. O soul, for the reverent man has perished from the earth, and there is none among men who does what is right: all are judged in blood, and the rest. […]

And the cart that is rolled is the one of which we read in Isaiah: The land of Moab shall be trampled down, as a threshing floor is trampled with carts. And in another place: I will make you, he says, like the new wheels of a cart with the teeth of saws, and you shall crush the mountains and grind the hills to pieces, so that, after you have crushed the mountains and hills, flight may perish from the swift, as Paul says: Do you not know that those who run in the stadium all run indeed, but one receives the prize. And in another place: You were running well; who hindered you, so that you should not obey the truth? Hence, fearing for himself as well, he says: Not that I have already received, or am perfect; […]

Behold, I will creak beneath you, as a cart loaded with hay creaks, and flight shall perish from the swift, and the mighty shall not hold his strength, and the strong shall not save his soul, and he who holds the bow shall not stand, and the swift of foot shall not be saved, and the rider of the horse shall not save his soul, and the strong of heart among the mighty shall flee naked in that day, says the Lord. LXX: Therefore behold, I will roll beneath you as a cart full of stubble is rolled, and flight shall perish from the runner, and the mighty shall not hold his might, and the fighter shall not save his soul, and the archer shall not endure, and the swift of foot shall not be able to be saved, and the horseman shall not save his soul, and his heart is found among the powerful, […]

He sometimes compares himself with deep condescension, on account of our infirmity, to objects without sense, as he says by the prophet, "Behold, I will shriek over you as a cart creaks when laden with hay." For since the life of the carnal is hay (as it is written, all flesh is hay), in that the Lord endures the life of the carnal he declares that he carries hay as a cart. And to creak under the weight of the hay is for him to bear with murmuring the burdens and iniquities of sinners. When therefore he applies to himself very unlike resemblances, we must carefully observe that some things of this kind are sometimes spoken of concerning God, on account of the effect of his doings, but sometimes to indicate the substance of his majesty.
2:13.s: MORALS ON THE BOOK OF JOB 6:32.7

2:14.t: There follows: And the mighty shall not hold his strength; not that he is mighty, but that he boasts of being mighty. Or he is the one who trusts in his own strength and not in the mercy of God, according to what is written: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the understanding of the prudent I will reject; not that true wisdom can perish and the understanding of the truth be rejected, but that the wisdom of those perishes who seem wise in their own eyes and trust in their own learning. The strong one too, or the fighter, who will not save his soul, is he who by no means possesses the armour of the Apostle: having a shield, but not of faith; girded about the loins, but not in truth; clothed with a breastplate, but not of righteousness; bearing a sword, but not of salvation. […]

2:15.t: The heretics too have archers, who, bending the bow in vain, will not be able to withstand the arrow of the Lord, who speaks through Isaiah: But I am like a chosen arrow in the quiver of the Lord. These are the archers of whom David also sings: Behold, sinners have bent the bow, they have made ready their arrows in the quiver, to shoot in the dark at the upright of heart. And the swift of foot, he says, shall not be saved: he who, because of the sharpness of his wit, runs about through the testimonies of the Scriptures and strives to crush the truth with the eloquence of orators or the sophisms of dialecticians; and in this he is tripped and falls, because he trusts not in the Lord but in his own feet. […]

2:16.t: And the strong also of heart among the mighty shall flee naked. This passage can be explained in two ways: either that he can escape for this reason, that he has stripped off the old man and the skin tunics of sins, and was weighed down by no burden; or, on the contrary, that because he is naked and has lost the garment of Christ, of which it is said in the Apostle too: Put on Christ Jesus, and in another place: If indeed, being clothed, we are not found naked, his strength will profit him nothing, but in the day of battle and contest he will flee from his pursuers and, unable to resist without the armour of the Apostle, will turn his back to the enemy.

3:1.t: Hear the word which the Lord has spoken concerning you, sons of Israel; concerning every kindred which I brought out of the land of Egypt, saying: Solely you have I known of all the kindreds of the earth; therefore I will visit upon you all your iniquities. LXX: Hear this word which the Lord has spoken concerning you, house of Israel, and against every tribe which I brought out of the land of Egypt, saying. Nevertheless, you have I known of all the tribes of the earth; therefore I will take vengeance upon you for all your wickednesses. […]

The word might be understood as having come against all of Israel, no longer taking Judah and Ephraim in part, but with the whole race gathered as if into one; for every tribe of Israel was brought up from Egypt. Therefore, with none being left out, he commands them to hear the things from God. And what were these things? For there are countless, he says, cities and countries throughout the whole world under heaven, and those in them are beyond number, but you from Israel out of all I have made chosen, I made myself manifest through many wonders, I delivered you from bitter and unbearable slavery, I declared you enviable and thrice-blessed, I have instructed you by law for what is pleasing to me, I have fortified you with my assistance, and I have brought you into the land promised […]

3:2.t: For this very cause God accuses the Israelites more vehemently, and shows that they were worthy of greater chastisement, because they sinned after so many honors had come to them from Him, saying in one place: "But you only have I known of all the families of the earth, therefore will I punish you for your iniquities," and again, "and I raised up of your sons for prophets, and of your young men for Nazarites;" and before the times of the prophets, wishing to show that sins receive sorer punishment by far when they occur in the case of the Priest than in the case of the laity, He enjoins as great a sacrifice to be offered for the Priest as for the whole people, and this amounts to a proof on his part, that the wounds of the Priesthood need more assistance—that is, as great as those […]

3:3.t: There are some who think that the first example contains a teaching: that two cannot walk together unless they have first agreed with each other in him who made both one, and the middle wall of the partition destroyed, and fashioned the two into one new man; and he made peace between them, and joined them with the bond of love, so that, when two are together, they may ask of the Father and obtain whatever they have asked. These are the two rods which are joined to each other in Ezekiel, and the two peoples, of the circumcision and of the Gentiles, of which the Lord speaks to Elijah: I have left for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal. And in another place God: I was found, he says, by those who did not seek me; […]

Will two walk together unless they have agreed? Will a lion roar in the forest unless he has prey? Will the lion's whelp give voice from his den unless he has seized something? Will a bird fall into the snare of the earth without a fowler? Will the snare be taken up from the earth before it has caught something? If the trumpet sounds in the city, will the people not be terrified? Will there be evil in the city which the Lord has not done, for the Lord God will not do a thing unless he has revealed his secret to his servants the prophets. The lion will roar, who will not fear? The Lord God has spoken, who will not prophesy? LXX: Will two walk together at all unless they have known each other? Will a lion bellow from his forest, having no prey? […]

He therefore accuses them, because they claimed that the prophets from Him did not convey words from above and from God; but rather they thought that things were being uttered from their own opinion, and that they were speaking things different from what seemed good to the Lord of all. For this reason He says, O foolish and senseless ones, will any of you become friends and walk the same path of life, not having known yourselves, or rather one another; that is, unless they have seen one another to be of the same character and like-minded? "For every creature loves its like, and a man will cleave to his like." And if this is true, how could I have accepted the prophets, as it were, into friendship and love, being holy Myself, if they too had not become holy? […]

3:4.t: But if they are separated by discord, at once the roaring lion will attack them, of whom the apostle Peter also says: Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour. This roaring lion does not move about in sown fields, not in vineyards, not in olive groves, nor among the fruit-bearing trees, which praise God, but where there are forests and untilled ground and wild beasts dwell. And not only will they lie open to the lion's bites, but the lion's whelp will seize them and lead them to his den, fleeing the light and making for the darkness. For everyone who sins loves the darkness and hates the light; of these we read in the psalm too: You have set darkness, and it became night; in it all the beasts of the forest will pass through. […]

Those who study the habits of wild beasts say that the lion, when it is in need of food, roams about powerfully through mountains and glens and forests, turning its eye this way and that, and seeking to catch something of the animals grazing in the woods. But when it sees something suitable for food, then it comes near and makes its attack, roaring terribly and harshly. Why then, He says, do you accuse God, because He makes the threat before the attack of terrible things? And why do you gnash your teeth at the prophets themselves, because they too have cried out against your impiety? For I am like a lion, He says, which is accustomed to roar before the hunt, all but threatening the attack beforehand, and the prophets are like cubs, imitating my custom. […]

3:5.t: The third punishment of those whom discord has separated is that they lose the wings by which they were formerly borne on high, and fall headlong from heaven to earth, and are held by the fowler, who is better called ἰξευτὴς, because with clinging birdlime he catches free birds which of their own will come down to earthly things. Of these it is written in Proverbs: Not unjustly are nets spread for birds. For just is the ruin of sinners, who, though they had the wings of a dove and ought to have flown through the air, were pressed down to earthly things by the weight of their sins, and through their own vice stuck fast to the birdlime. Of this we read in the Apostle: He who cleaves to a harlot becomes one body with her. […]

The discourse is now made by way of comparison. For fowlers most skillfully bring down the sparrows that have settled in the plants, and with snares, on the other hand, some crush what is caught. But the discourse now seems to signify through the sparrows those who are accustomed to think lofty things, the boastful in mind and arrogant in spirit, and not enduring to be brought down with the lowly; and through those caught in snares, the lovers of earthly things, and those who seek only carnal and fattening things. And God again compares himself to a fowler and a snare, bringing the proud down to the earth, and as it were crushing and hunting for punishment those who mind only the things on earth. […]

3:6.t: The fifth punishment is that of those who have abandoned the peace which surpasses all understanding, and which the Lord, as he went to the Father, left to the apostles, saying: My peace I give to you, my peace I leave to you: that, though set in the city of the Lord, they are terrified by the sound of the trumpet. For whatever is said in the holy Scriptures is a threatening trumpet, piercing the ears of believers with a great voice. If we are righteous, we are summoned by the trumpet of Christ to blessedness; if sinners, we hear what torments we are going to suffer. But the evil which the Lord does in the city is not the contrary of virtue, but affliction and torment, of which we read: Sufficient to the day is its own evil, that is, tribulation and distress. […]

Germanus: We often read in holy Scripture that God has created evil or brought it upon men, as is this passage: "There is none beside Me. I am the Lord, and there is none else: I form the light and create darkness, I make peace, and create evil." And again: "Shall there be evil in a city which the Lord hath not done?"

Theodore: Sometimes holy Scripture is wont by an improper use of terms to use "evils "for "affliction;" not that these are properly and in their nature evils, but because they are imagined to be evils by those on whom they are brought for their good. For when divine judgment is reasoning with men it must speak with the language and feelings of men. […]

But perhaps you say that the outcome of these matters grieves you not moderately. Will there then be an affliction in a city, perchance, which the Lord has not done? It is like as if one should say: Will there then be anyone among men able to afflict a city either with diseases or sieges or destructions of crops or even in some other such way? But if no one of men could do such things, and it lies rather in the authority and power of God, why are you angry with those who announce it beforehand? And yet it is necessary to repent, and by inclinations to this to appease him the one who is grieved and has the power to harm those who have sinned. […]

His permission, therefore, is usually spoken of in the Holy Scripture as His energy and work. Nay, even when He says that God creates evil things, and that there is no evil in a city that the Lord hath not done, he does not mean by these words that the Lord is the cause of evil, but the word ‘evil’ is used in two ways, with two meanings. For sometimes it means what is evil by nature, and this is the opposite of virtue and the will of God: and sometimes it means that which is evil and oppressive to our sensation, that is to say, afflictions and calamities. Now these are seemingly evil because they are painful, but in reality are good. For to those who understand they become ambassadors of conversion and salvation. The Scripture says that of these God is the Author. […]
3:6.s: An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith, Book 4, Chapter 19

3:7.t: There follows: The Lord God will not do a thing unless he has revealed his secret, or his correction, to his servants the prophets; not that God reveals to the prophets everything that he does in heaven or has already done before, but what he is going to do on earth. He revealed to Noah his servant that he was going to bring on the flood. He revealed to Abraham and Lot his servants that Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim were going to burn. He revealed to Joseph the interpretation of the dream of the seven years of famine in Egypt, and to the prophet Jonah the overthrow of Nineveh, so that those who heard of the punishments to come might either repent and avoid the torments, or, if they scorned them, be punished more justly. […]

3:8.t: The lion, he says, will roar, and who will not fear? The Lord God has spoken, who will not prophesy? The word who is taken in this passage not for the impossible, but for the rare. For he will not fear, and he will not prophesy, who because of his hardness has scorned to hear the Lord. And the sense according to the history is this: If at the voice of the lion all things tremble and the whole nature of living creatures is terrified, shall we, when God commands us to speak and announce to the people the punishments to come, not prophesy? Shall we not speak? […]

"Lord, you have been our refuge." Therefore we have recourse to you. Our healing shall be from you, for our evil is from ourselves. Because we have abandoned you, you have abandoned us to ourselves. May we therefore be found in you, for in ourselves we had been lost. "Lord, you have been our refuge." Why, my brethren, should we doubt that the Lord will make us gentle if we submit ourselves to be tamed by him? You have tamed the lion, which you did not create. Will your Creator be unable to tame you? What is the source of your power to tame such savage beasts? Are you their equal in bodily strength? By what power then have you been able to tame such huge beasts? The so-called beasts of burden are wild by nature, for if untamed they could not be endured. […]

"A lion will roar, and who will not be afraid? The Lord God has spoken, and who will not prophesy?" It is not the prophets, he says, who bring on the things that come from wrath; how could they? For they are also human in nature, just like you, but they have been honored by God by learning all the things that He might wish to fulfill, and to bring upon cities and lands either good things, perhaps, or things that are accustomed to cause pain. But perhaps you say to this: Let them learn, if you wish; let them be enriched by you with the knowledge of future events; let all the mysteries be made clear to them; but let them speak to no one, nor let them sound anything in the ears of those who reject them. What then is the reply to this from God? […]

3:9.t: Make it heard in the houses of Azotus, and in the houses of the land of Egypt; and say: Gather yourselves upon the mountains of Samaria, and see the many madnesses in the midst of her, those who suffer calumnies in her inner chambers; and they did not know how to do what is right, says the Lord, treasuring up iniquity and plunder in their houses. LXX: Announce to the regions among the Assyrians, and to the regions of the land of Egypt; and say: Gather yourselves upon the mountain of Samaria, and see many wonders in the midst of her, and the oppression in her; and she did not know what things are to come before her, says the Lord, who treasure up iniquity and misery in their regions. […]

3:11.t: Therefore thus says the Lord God: The land shall be afflicted and surrounded, and your strength shall be pulled down from you, and your houses shall be plundered. LXX: Therefore thus says the Lord God: Tyre, and your land round about, shall be deserted, and he will pull down your strength from you, and your regions shall be plundered. In place of Tyre, which in the Hebrew is written with two letters, sade and res, and is called Sor, as Aquila and the Seventy likewise translated it, the Hebrew who instructed me in the holy Scriptures interpreted tribulation; nor do we reject his opinion, because Symmachus too, who is not accustomed to follow the κακοζηλίαν (affectation) of words but the order of the understanding, says siege and encircling of the land. […]

3:12.t: If you have any hope of salvation; if you have the least thought of God, or any desire for good things to come; if you have any fear of the chastisements reserved for the impenitent, awake without delay, lift up your eyes to heaven, come to your senses, cease from your wickedness, shake off the stupor that enwraps you, make a stand against the foe who has struck you down. Make an effort to rise from the ground. Remember the good Shepherd who will follow and rescue you. Though it be but two legs or a lobe of an ear, spring back from the beast that has wounded you. Remember the mercies of God and how He cures with oil and wine. Do not despair of salvation. Recall your recollection of how it is written in the Scriptures that he who is falling rises and he who turns away returns; […]

Thus says the Lord: As if a shepherd should rescue from the mouth of the lion two legs, or the tip of an ear, so shall the sons of Israel be rescued who dwell in Samaria in the region of the couch and on the pallet of Damascus. LXX: Thus says the Lord: As if a shepherd should tear away from the mouth of the lion two legs, or the tip of an ear, so shall the sons of Israel be torn away who dwell in Samaria over against the tribe and in Damascus. At the beginning of Amos, where we discussed those little verses: The Lord will roar from Zion, and from Jerusalem he will utter his voice; […]

3:13.t: Hear and testify in the house of Jacob, says the Lord God of hosts, that in the day when I begin to visit the transgressions of Israel upon him, I will visit also upon the altars of Bethel; and the horns of the altar shall be cut off and shall fall to the ground; and I will strike the winter house with the summer house; and the houses of ivory shall perish; and many houses shall be scattered, says the Lord. LXX: Priests, hear: testify to the house of Jacob, says the Lord God Almighty, that in the day when I avenge the iniquities of Israel upon him, I will avenge also upon the altars of Bethel; and the horns of the altar shall be undermined and shall fall upon the ground. I will confound and strike the winged house upon the summer house, and the houses of ivory shall perish; […]

3:14.t: When I begin, he says, to visit the transgressions, or impieties, of the house of Israel, and to render to them what they deserve, and the time of captivity has come, then the altars of Bethel shall be destroyed, where the golden calves were, and the horns of the altar shall be cut off, the altar which was split apart when Jeroboam too stretched out his hand, and they shall crash to the ground, broken, as the Assyrian lays waste.

When the Lord begins to visit the transgressions of Israel, which formerly beheld God with the mind, he will visit also upon the altars of Bethel, not the one altar which the Church has, but the very many altars of the heretics. For they have as many altars as schisms. He will cut off also the horns of the altar which in their pride they boast that they possess as the one altar. And their horns, that is, their arrogance, will fall to the ground; and he will strike the winter house, those heretics who toil in continence and fasts, in dry fasts and sleeping on the ground, among whom are Tatian and Mani; and the summer house, such as the Nicolaitans and the Eunomians, and the new followers of an old heresy, who for the gluttony of the belly admit every pleasure. […]

3:15.t: And I will strike, he says, the winter house with the summer house, which we can take simply according to the letter: that they were of such great wealth that they had double houses, winter ones and summer ones, of which some faced the north and others the south, so that according to the variety of the seasons they might secure a temperate measure of cold and heat and of the sky. We can call the winter house the kingdom of Israel, in which there was coldness of religion and of the worship of God, and various whirlwinds of the winds, and savage storm; and the summer house, Judah and Jerusalem, in which was the temple, and burnt offerings were offered morning and evening, and the warmth of religion flourished. […]

4:1.t: Hear this word, you fat cows, who are on the mountain of Samaria; who do calumny to the needy, and crush the poor, who say to your masters: Bring, and we will drink. The Lord God has sworn by his holy one that behold, days shall come upon you, and they shall lift you up on poles, and your remnants in boiling pots; and you shall go out through the openings, one against another, and you shall be cast into Armon, says the Lord. LXX: Hear this word, you cows of Basanitis, who are on the mountain of Samaria, who oppress the poor and trample the needy, who say to your masters: Give us, that we may drink. The Lord swears by his holy ones that behold, days shall come upon you, and they shall take you up in arms; and those who are with you, in pots, pestilent traders; […]

Now the word of the Lord which the cows of Bashan are commanded to hear is, according to the tropology we have begun, addressed to the heretics, who, serving the belly and gluttony, are rightly called very fat cows, or cows of ignominy; for this is what Bashan means, that is, αἰσχύνη; and if we wished to call it confusion, we should be interpreting Babylon rather than Bashan. These fat cows, or cows of ignominy and dry, for Bashan is understood in this sense too, are on the mountain of Samaria, to which it is also said in Hosea: Take away your calf, Samaria. And again in the same prophet: For your calf was a deceiver, Samaria; and they are on the mountain of Samaria for this reason, that they are always lifted up into pride and promise themselves lofty things. […]

4:2.t: And so the Lord swore by his holy one, whether by himself, or by the Son, or by the temple, or by everyone who is holy and is called the temple of God, that a day is to come not far off, nor after many ages, but already imminent: the day of captivity and distress, in which the cows are lifted up on poles, and their remnants in boiling pots, for which both in the Hebrew and in Aquila is written in cauldrons of little fish. For the poles too, which in Hebrew are called sannoth, Aquila interpreted shields, Symmachus and the LXX arms, Theodotion alone δόρατα; following him, we have interpreted poles or spears. […]

And the Lord your God swears by his holy one against the cows that are slaves to fattening and feasts, or he swears by his holy ones, that days shall come upon them, days of judgment and of punishments; so that, carrying them in their arms, they may put them, and those who are with them, into cauldrons, or carry them; and either the cows themselves are pestilent traders, or those who come to carry them; and they are cast out naked, seeing one another, and are cast upon mount Remmam, says the Lord God. For we must speak also according to the LXX, lest we seem to have set them out in vain. […]

4:3.t: And what follows: And you shall go out through the openings, one against another, can be explained thus: The way of captivity lies open to you, and when your cauldrons have been burnt out, you shall go out one against another; according to the idiom of the Hebrews, who, for what we say mutually or in turn, say woman and woman, that is, one against another. And you shall be cast, he says, into the places of Armenia which are called Armona. Finally Symmachus interpreted: And you shall be cast into Armenia, for which the Seventy translated mount Remmam, Aquila mount Armona, Theodotion mount Mona, the Fifth edition the lofty mount.

4:4.t: This we have said according to the Hebrew; let us pass on to the LXX translators, and discuss briefly what seems to us according to anagogy in each point; for the size of the books does not allow it, if we should wish to say both things in each edition. You entered into Bethel, that is, into the house of God, which is understood as the Church, and you acted impiously against the Lord, trampling on his precepts. And in Gilgal, which is interpreted revelation or wallowing-place, you multiplied impieties, claiming for yourselves the knowledge of the holy Scriptures, and while you are lifted up into pride, you have rolled down into the lowest depths of the mire. […]

Come to Bethel, and act impiously; to Gilgal, and multiply transgression; and bring your victims in the morning, your tithes on three days. And sacrifice praise from what is leavened, and call for voluntary offerings, and proclaim them. For so you have willed, sons of Israel, says the Lord God. Therefore I also have given you numbness of teeth in all your cities, and want of bread in all your places; and you have not returned to me, says the Lord. LXX: You entered into Bethel, and acted unjustly; in Gilgal you multiplied acting impiously, and you brought in your sacrifices in the morning, your tithes on the third day. And they read the law outside, and called upon confessions. Proclaim that the sons of Israel have loved these things, says the Lord God. […]

It is not enough to make a true solemnity of the heart. From this must follow good works. What value is there in partaking of his body and blood with our mouths if we oppose him with our wicked practices? And so Moses required that "unleavened bread with wild herbs" is to be eaten. One who eats bread without leaven does virtuous deeds without corrupting them with vainglory, and fulfills the precepts of mercy with no addition of sin, not perversely destroying what he properly accomplishes. In reproof of some who had mingled the leaven of sin with their good deeds, the Lord spoke by the voice of the prophet: "Come to Bethel and behave wickedly," and shortly after, "And make a sacrifice of praise of that which is unleavened." […]

4:5.t: Nor are the heretics, of whom and to whom this is said, content with this limit of impiety, but they read the law of God outside, withdrawing from the Church, and tried to join confessions and testimonies to each of their dogmas, which they feigned with a perverse heart; or they sacrificed from what is leavened, concerning which it is said in the Gospel: Beware of the leaven, that is, the teaching of the Pharisees. And they did these things not by error, but by design; not by a chance will, but with the fullest affection for their forebears.

They had also mixed this leaven of sin into their good action, to whom the Lord spoke through the voice of the prophet in rebuke: "Come to Bethel and act impiously." And after a few words: "And sacrifice praise from what is leavened." For he offers praise from what is leavened who prepares a sacrifice to God from robbery.

4:6.t: Wherefore I too have given you numbness of teeth, as the LXX translated, whom we have followed in this place because of the simplicity of the word, or cleanness of teeth, as Aquila and Symmachus translated, so as to show by clean teeth the greatness of the famine. And I caused want of bread, not in one city, but in all your cities, nor in one place, but in all your places. And though I have done this, not punishing, but granting an occasion for repentance, not even so have you returned to me, says the Lord.

Hence the Lord threatens vengeance upon them: I will give, he says, you numbness of teeth, which in Greek is called γομφιασμός. For if anyone, according to Ezekiel, eats a sour grape, his teeth will be numbed; so that those who make ill use of the testimonies of the holy Scriptures, and eat them unripe and without their sweetness, lose the strength of their teeth, so that they cannot grind hard food and pass into the belly what would profit the whole body. This numbness of teeth and want of food I will give both in all your cities and in all your places, so that you may suffer a famine of the word of God, and of that bread which came down from heaven, and of which it is written in the psalms: Man ate the bread of angels. […]

4:7.t: I also withheld the rain from you, when there were still three months left until the harvest. And I rained upon one city, and upon another city I did not rain. One part was rained upon, and the part upon which I did not rain withered. And two and three cities came to one city to drink water, and they were not satisfied; and you did not return to me, says the Lord. LXX: And I held back the rain from you three months before the vintage; and I will rain upon one city, and upon one city I will not rain. One part will be watered, and the part upon which I shall not rain will dry up. And two and three cities will gather into one city to drink water, and they will not be satisfied; and you have not returned to me, says the Lord. […]

4:9.t: I struck you with scorching wind and with mildew. The multitude of your gardens and of your vineyards, your olive groves and your fig groves, the caterpillar devoured, and you did not return to me, says the Lord. LXX: I struck you with burning heat and with mildew. You multiplied your gardens, your vineyards, and your figs, and your olive groves the caterpillar devoured, and not even so were you converted to me, says the Lord. Not only did I do the former things in order to correct you, but whatever was left over from the drought I struck with scorching wind and with mildew. For 'scorching wind' Aquila and Symmachus and Theodotion translated ἀνεμοφθορίαν; the Seventy πύρωσιν, which we can call burning. […]

4:10.t: I sent death upon you in the way of Egypt, I struck your young men with the sword, even to the captivity of your horses. And I made the stench of your camps rise into your nostrils, and you did not return to me, says the Lord. LXX: I sent forth death upon you in the way of Egypt, and I killed your young men with the sword, together with the captivity of your horses. And I brought out your camps in fire in my wrath, and not even so did you return to me, says the Lord. Israel is instructed by every kind of scourge and torment; […]

4:11.t: See how God, through His love of goodness, seeks repentance; and by means of the plan He pursues of threatening silently, shows His own love for man. "I will avert," He says, "My face from them, and show what shall happen to them." For where the face of the Lord looks, there is peace and rejoicing; but where it is averted, there is the introduction of evil.

Whence also, that there might be no doubt but that it was He who was the guest of Abraham on the destruction of the people of Sodom, it is declared: "Then the Lord rained upon Sodom and upon Gomorrha fire and brimstone from the Lord out of heaven." For thus also said the prophet in the person of God: "I have overthrown you, as the Lord overturned Sodom and Gomorrha." Therefore the Lord overturned Sodom, that is, God overturned Sodom; but in the overturning of Sodom, the Lord rained fire from the Lord. And this Lord was the God seen by Abraham; and this God was the guest of Abraham, certainly seen because He was also touched. […]

[Passage quoted, Amos iv. ii.]

AND here the Lord Himself says that some God has caused the destruction of Sodom, since He Himself must plainly be a different Being from the One of Whom He speaks. Therefore two Lords stands out in the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, when the Lord rained the fire of the Lord on them. You also, he says, will suffer a destruction such as Sodom underwent for its unnatural wickedness, and even so did not turn to Me. Scripture generally regards the future as past, so that we must understand the past to be meant in spite of the tense. The future "I will overthrow" must be understood for the past "I overthrew," and "ye will not turn," for "ye did turn." […]
4:11.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 5, Chapter 23

4:11.t: I overthrew you as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you became like a brand snatched from the burning, and you did not return to me, says the Lord. LXX: I overthrew you as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and you became like a brand plucked out of the fire, and not even so were you converted to me, says the Lord. It is the last remedy, both for the ten tribes and for the heretics and for all sinners, that, after he has sent death in the way of Egypt, and struck their young men with the sword, and consumed their horses, and made the stench of their camps rise into their nostrils, and still they have not returned to him, he should overthrow them as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah; […]

There are also other sorts of vengeance, with which some who have overpassed the bounds of wickedness are smitten in this life, as we read that Dathan and Abiram or Korah were punished, or above all, those of whom the Apostle speaks: "Wherefore God gave them up to vile passions and a reprobate mind:" and this must be counted worse than all other punishments. For of these the Psalmist says: "They are not in the labours of men; neither shall they be scourged like other men." […]

In this he was probably suggesting to us the eventual sacking that happened in the time of Jeremiah by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, who took the whole of Judea, set fire even to Jerusalem itself and its neighboring cities and towns, pulled down the divine Temple, took captive the survivors from the fighting, and as a glorious conqueror went back home with the captives, who finally returned to Judea at the completion of the period of 70 years.

4:12.t: I gave numbness to your teeth, and you did not return to me, says the Lord. I withheld the rain from you, and I rained upon one city, and upon another I did not rain, and two and three cities came to one to drink water, and they were not satisfied, and not even so did you return to me, says the Lord. I struck you with scorching wind, and with mildew your gardens and vineyards and olive groves and fig groves, and you did not return to me, says the Lord. I sent death upon you in the way of Egypt, and I struck your young men with the sword, and I made the stench of your camps rise into your nostrils, and you did not return to me, says the Lord. […]

But if we read according to Symmachus and Aquila: These things I will do to you, Israel, afterwards, and when I have done these things to you, prepare to oppose your God Israel, it is to be understood thus: In order to correct you I did the things which the preceding discourse describes; and because you were unwilling to return to me, I will do to you the things that are contained in my secret counsel. You killed the servants whom I had sent to you; last of all I will send my Son; but you, according to your custom, by which you have always resisted the will of God, prepare yourself to contradict and oppose your God, according to that which is written: Behold, this one is set for the fall and for the rising again of many, and for a sign which shall be contradicted. […]

Therefore I will do these things to you, Israel; but after I have done these things to you, prepare to meet your God, Israel; for behold, he who forms the mountains, and creates the wind, and announces to man his speech, who makes the morning mist, and treads upon the heights of the earth, the Lord God of hosts is his name. LXX: Therefore thus will I do to you, Israel; nevertheless, because I will do thus to you, prepare to call upon your God, Israel. For behold, he who establishes the thunder, and creates the spirit, and announces to men his Christ, making the morning and the mist, and ascending upon the heights of the earth, the Lord God Almighty is his name. […]

Since initial measures did not suffice, He proceeded to an overthrow similar to the Sodomites; this was the kind of thing, as he said, that was inflicted on them by divine wrath. Therefore prepare to call upon your God, O Israel: Since he did not benefit from being chastised, let him prepare himself for an encounter with God, accepting repentance and adopting a lifestyle calculated to appease Him.

4:13.t:
[Passage quoted, Amos. iv. 12—v. 2.]

God now proclaiming the Christ by name the seventh time is said to "strengthen the thunder" and "to create the wind," the proclamation of the Gospel being called thunder from its being heard by all men, and similarly the spirit that Christ breathed on His apostles is meant; and also the Saviour's sojourn among men has clearly fulfilled the prophecy in which God is said to make "morning" and "mist" together, morning for those that receive salvation, but for the Jews that disbelieve in Him the contrary. On whom also Scripture foretells an extreme curse, adding a lamentation for the Jewish race, which actually overtook them immediately after their impiety against our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. […]
4:13.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 4, Chapter 16

4:13.t: It is the custom of Scripture to call firmament all that is strong and unyielding. It even uses the word to denote the condensation of the air: He, it says, who strengthens the thunder. Scripture means by the strengthening of the thunder, the strength and resistance of the wind, which, enclosed in the hollows of the clouds, produces the noise of thunder when it breaks through with violence.
4:13.s: The Hexaemeron, Homily 3: On the Firmament

4:13.t: Nor does it escape my notice that heretics have been prone to object that the Holy Spirit appears to be a creature, because many of them use as an argument for establishing their impiety that passage of Amos, where he spoke of the blowing of the wind, as the words of the prophet made clear. For you read thus: "Behold, I am he that establishes the thunder and creates the wind and declare unto man his Christ, that make light and mist, and ascend upon high places, the Lord God Almighty is his name."

But if any one thinks that the word of the prophet is to be explained with reference to the Holy Spirit, because it is said, "declaring unto men his Christ," he will explain it more easily of the Lord's Sun of justice. For if it troubles you that he said Spirit, and therefore you think that this cannot well be explained of the mystery of the taking of human nature, read on in the Scriptures, and you will find that all agrees most excellently with Christ. Of [Christ] it is thoroughly fitting to think that he established the thunders by his coming, that is, the force and sound of the heavenly Scriptures, by the thunder, as it were, of which our minds are struck with astonishment, so that we learn to be afraid and pay respect to the heavenly oracles.

He it is who establishes the thunder, or makes firm the mountains, at whose voice the hinges of the heavens and the foundations of the earth are shaken. He it is who creates the spirit, which in this place we understand not as the Holy Spirit, as the heretics suppose, but as the wind, or the spirit of man, because no one knows what is in a man except the spirit which is in him; and the Spirit himself intercedes for us with unspeakable groanings. Or certainly by 'spirit' we ought to understand the soul, according to that which is written: You will take away their spirit, and they will fail, and they will return to their dust. And: Father, into your hands I commend my spirit, and saying this he breathed his last. […]

This is Amos the third in order, who also was privileged to tell of the coming of the Lord Christ and in these words: Lo! I am he that confirms the thunder and that creates the wind and that announces to men his Anointed.

5:1.t: Hear this word, which I raise over you as a lament. The house of Israel has fallen; it will not again rise. The virgin Israel is cast down into her land; there is no one to raise her up. LXX: Hear this word, which I will take up over you as a lament. The house of Israel has fallen; it will not any more rise again. The virgin Israel is cast down upon her land; there is no one to raise her up. As far as concerns the order of the letter and the truth of the history begun, the ten tribes, which are called Israel, once led into captivity, by no means returned afterwards to their own land.
