And the people of Israel is called a virgin, not because it remained in the purity of virginity, but because it was once joined to the Lord like a virgin. […]

5:2.t: Consider and observe, my hearer, that if God had given a hope to Sodom and to her fellows, He would not have overthrown them with fire and brimstone, the sign of the last day of the world, but would have delivered them over to one of the kingdoms to be chastised. As it is written that when Jeremiah caused the nations and kingdoms to drink the cup of wrath, he said concerning each one of the cities, that after they shall drink the cup, I will turn back the captivity of Elam, of Tyre, of Zidon, of the children of Ammon, and of Moab, and of Edom. Concerning each one of these kingdoms he said:—In the last days I well turn back her captivity. […]

If, then, the apostle, who was a chosen vessel separated unto the gospel of Christ, by reason of the pricks of the flesh and the allurements of vice keeps his body and brings it into subjection, lest when he has preached to others he may himself be a cast away; and yet, for all that, sees another law in his members warring against the law of his mind, and bringing him into captivity to the law of sin; if after nakedness, fasting, hunger, imprisonment, scourging and other torments, he turns back to himself and cries, "Oh, wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" do you fancy that you ought to lay aside apprehension? See to it that God say not some day of you, "The virgin of Israel is fallen, and there is none to raise her up." […]

But if, as we have said, the lament is over those who repent, and repentance restores health to the wound, how is it said according to the Seventy: The house of Israel has fallen, it will rise no more. The virgin Israel has strayed in her land, there is no one to raise her up? This can be resolved thus: after the house of Israel has collapsed by its own will, it will by no means recover its former dignity; after the virgin Israel has strayed in her land, she will no longer be able to find one to raise her up. And consider the proper meanings of the words. He who is a house, and is counted in the crowd, is said to fall. But he who is of the number of the virgins, if he strays, even for a light sin, will not be able to be raised up; […]

5:3.t: For thus says the Lord God: The city from which a thousand went out, there shall be left in it a hundred; and from which a hundred went out, there shall be left in it ten, in the house of Israel. LXX: likewise. The divine word gives the reasons why the house of Israel, falling, does not rise again, and the virgin Israel, straying, or cast down upon the land, has no one to raise her up. The city, he says, from which a thousand went out, there shall be left in it a hundred; and from which a hundred went out, there shall be left in it ten, in the house of Israel; so that where once there had been a multitude, because of the excessive devastation scarcely a tenth part remains. […]

5:4.t: For thus says the Lord to the house of Israel: Seek me, and you shall live; and do not seek Bethel, and do not enter into Gilgal, and do not pass over to Beersheba; for Gilgal shall be led captive, and Bethel shall be useless. LXX: For thus says the Lord to the house of Israel: Seek me, and you shall live; and do not seek Bethel, and do not go into Gilgal, and do not pass over upon the well of the oath; for Gilgal shall be led captive, and Bethel shall be as though it were not. It is the custom of the Scriptures always to join glad things to adverse ones, and after God has threatened sad things, he calls to repentance those whom he has frightened, according to that which we read in Isaiah: Woe, sinful nation, a people full of offences, a most wicked seed, unjust sons. […]

5:5.t: And do not seek Bethel, in which was the golden calf, and Gilgal, the place of idolatry, of which I have also said above: All their wickedness is in Gilgal. And you shall not pass over to Beersheba. Beautifully he says: you shall not pass over to Beersheba, that is, to the well of the oath, where the tribe of Judah, whenever it went astray, had been accustomed to worship idols. But Israel raged in the worship of images to such a degree that, by no means content with its own idols, it passed over to those of others. Finally, Gilgal, he says, shall be led captive, and Bethel shall be useless, or not subsisting at all, when the idols in it have been overthrown. […]

5:6.t: Therefore, while there is time, look to the true and eternal salvation, and, since the end of the world is now at hand, out of fear of God turn your minds to God. Let not your powerless and vain dominion in the world over the just and the meek delight you. Remember that in the fields the tares and the darnel have dominion over the cultivated and fruitful corn, and you should not say that evils happen because your gods are not worshiped by us. But you should realize that this is God's anger, this is God's censure, so that he who is not recognized for his blessings may at least be recognized for his judgments. "Seek God, and your soul shall live." Acknowledge God even though it is late. […]
5:6.s: Treatise V. An Address to Demetrianus 23

5:6.t: Seek the Lord and live, lest perhaps the house of Joseph be burned like fire; and it will devour, and there will be no one to quench Bethel. LXX: Seek the Lord and live, lest perhaps the house of Joseph be kindled like fire; and it devour it, and there be no one to quench the house of Israel. Just as it is said in the person of God: Seek me, and you shall live, so the prophet speaks about the Lord, that they should seek him and live. For in seeking the Lord they begin to live; but if they have not sought him, and for that reason have not lived, at once the house of Joseph will be kindled like fire. […]

5:7.t: You who turn judgment into wormwood and leave righteousness on the earth; him who makes Arcturus and Orion, and turns darkness into morning, and changes day into night. Who calls the waters of the sea and pours them out upon the face of the earth: the Lord is his name. Who smiles devastation upon the strong, and brings plundering upon the mighty. LXX: Who makes judgment on high and has set righteousness on the earth; who makes all things, and transforms them, and turns the shadow of death into morning, and darkens the day into night. Who calls the water of the sea and pours it out upon the face of the earth: the Lord God Almighty is his name. Who divides crushing upon strength, and brings misery upon the fortress. […]

Let us speak also according to the LXX: God makes judgment on high, when he judges truth and renders to each according to his work; and everyone who is an imitator of God, and desires to be his son, and to be perfect, as his Father who dwells in heaven is perfect, makes judgment on high, and does not imitate that judge who did not fear God, and did not respect man, and by the perversity of his judgment did not lift his sentence up to heaven, but dragged it down to the depths. And as for what follows: And has set righteousness on the earth, we ought to take it according to this, that he gave us Christ, his righteousness, and did not cast it away but set it down on the earth, so that, all iniquity being overcome, he might make us heavenly from earthly. […]

5:8.t: When I think of the past tempest, and of the present calm, I cease not saying, "Blessed be God, who maketh all things, and changeth them; who hath brought light out of darkness; who leadeth to the gates of hell, and bringeth back; who chastiseth, but killeth not." And this I desire you too to repeat constantly, and never to desist. For if He hath benefitted us by deeds, what pardon shall we deserve, if we do not requite Him even by words. Therefore, I exhort that we never cease to give Him thanks; since if we are grateful for the former benefits, it is plain that we shall enjoy others also, which are greater. […]

See how highly God has honored us, in committing to us so excellent a frame. I made heaven and earth, He says, and to you I give the power of creation. Make your earth heaven. For it is in thy power. "I am He that maketh and transformeth all things" (Amos v. 8, Sept.), saith God of Himself. And He hath given to men a similar power; as a painter, being an affectionate father, teaches his own art to his son. I formed thy body beautiful, he says, but I give thee the power of forming something better. Make thy soul beautiful. I said, "Let the earth bring forth grass, and every fruitful tree." Do thou also say, Let this earth bring forth its proper fruit, and what thou willest to produce will be produced. "I make the summer and the cloud. I create the lightning and the wind." […]

But what this righteousness is, the following verse shows: Him who makes Arcturus and Orion, and turns darkness into morning, and changes day into night. He of whom he had said above: Forming the mountains, and creating the wind, and announcing to man his speech, making the morning mist, and stepping upon the high places of the earth: the Lord God of hosts is his name, he it is who is the Creator of Arcturus, which in Hebrew is called Chima, and by Symmachus and Theodotion is rendered εἰς πλειάδα (the Pleiades), which is commonly called Boötes. And as for what follows, Orion, which in Hebrew is called Chasil, Symmachus translated it absolutely as stars, Theodotion as the evening star. […]

But in saying: Making all things and transforming them, they comprehend Arcturus and Orion in one word, neglecting to carry over the proper sense of the names into the Greek language. And God transforms all things when he makes heavenly things from earthly, and bestows on men the likeness of angels; when the moon will glow with the brightness of the sun, and the sun will have sevenfold light; when man, animal and weak and corruptible, is transformed into one spiritual and strong and incorrupt, changing his glory, not his nature; when those who understand will shine like the splendour of the firmament, and what is written will be fulfilled: One is the glory of the sun, another the glory of the moon, another the glory of the stars. For star differs from star in brightness; […]

5:9.t: And as for what follows: Who smiles devastation upon the strong, he returns to the present time. And the order is: he who is the Creator of all things also threatens captivity upon Samaria, and brings plundering upon the mighty, since it turns judgment into wormwood and leaves righteousness on the earth. Where we have said, who smiles, Aquila translated ὁ μειδιῶν. And μειδίαμα is properly said of what we can call a smiling, when someone is angry and, with his lips parted a little, pretends to smile, so as to show the greatness of his anger.

This God also divides crushing upon strength, so as to make weak those who are wickedly strong, and so that they can imitate the Apostle, who says: When I am weak, then I am stronger. For the sons of this world are more prudent than the sons of light in their own generation. The strength of the body is the weakness of the soul, and again the strength of the soul is the weakness of the body. Therefore the Lord, who dispenses all things by reason and does all things by true judgment, divides crushing upon the strong enemy, so as to bring misery upon the fortress which raises itself up against the knowledge of God. Of which we also read in Proverbs: The wise man entered strong cities and destroyed the fortress in which the ungodly trusted. […]

5:10.t: They take the two sons as types of two peoples, the elder Jewish, the younger Christian.… But if I show that the Jew does not fit the type represented by the elder son, it will be admitted, in consequence, that the Christian is not typified by the younger. Admittedly, the Jew is called a "son" and an "elder son" since he is first by adoption, and although he resents the Christian's reconciliation with God his Father (this is a point which our opponents seize upon most eagerly), yet the statement "Behold, how many years I serve you and I have never transgressed your commandment" cannot be one which the Jew makes to the Father. For when was Judah not a transgressor of the law? […]

They hated him who rebukes in the gate, and abhorred him who speaks perfectly. LXX: They hated him who reproves in the gates, and abhorred the holy word. These upon whom God smiles devastation, and brings plundering upon them, who are strong in evil and mighty to oppress, hated him who rebukes in the gate, that is, in court: either me, or the other prophets who have been sent to them; and him who speaks perfectly, or the immaculate word, as Symmachus translated, or the holy speech, as Theodotion and the LXX rendered. […]

5:11.t: We can say this very thing of the heretics as well, who plunder the poor man, or strike his head with a clenched hand: for this is what κατεκονδύλιζον means in Greek, according to what we read above, striking the poor upon the head. For the heretics strike none but the poor man, who cannot withstand the threat, and not in his other members, but in the ruling part of the heart and in the truth of faith. The poor, I think, are those who, content with a simple faith, are unable to answer the malice of the heretics. But whatever good work they have also prepared as gifts for God, unless they resist the adversaries, they will lose in the time of battle and contest; […]

Therefore, because you plundered the poor man and took choice spoil from him, you shall build houses of squared stone and shall not dwell in them; you shall plant most lovely vineyards and shall not drink their wine. For I have known your many crimes and your strong sins, enemies of the just, taking a gift and pressing down the poor in the gate; therefore the prudent man shall keep silent at that time, for it is an evil time. LXX: Therefore, because you struck the poor with the fist, and received choice gifts from them, you have built houses of hewn stones, and you shall not dwell in them; you have planted desirable vineyards, and you shall not drink their wine; for I have known your many impieties and your strong sins; […]

And this you may learn from what He Himself says thereupon by the mouth of the holy prophets; "Therefore because you have bruised the heads of the poor, and taken from them chosen gifts, you shall build houses of carved stone, but you shall not dwell therein: and you shall plant desirable vineyards, but you shall not drink of their wine. For I know your many wickednesses, and mighty are your sins." And again, "Woe unto those who add house to house, and join field to field, that they may take away something from their neighbour. Will you dwell alone in the earth? For these things have been heard in the ears of the Lord of hosts. For though your houses be many, they shall be a desolation: though they be great and fair, there shall be none to inhabit them. […]
5:11.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

5:12.t: Here knowledge is not to be understood according to what we read elsewhere: The Lord knew those who are his, but in the sense that nothing is hidden from God, and that he knows all the secrets of sinners. I have known, he says, many impieties, which are not only many but also strong and oppressing, or trampling on righteousness itself, or on him who is just. And you receive, he says, exchange, for which all likewise translated ἐξίλασμα, that is, propitiation, and we said gift; but ἄλλαγμα, according to the idiom of the Scriptures, means a price, as we also read in the Gospel: Or what exchange shall a man give for his soul? […]

5:13.t: Therefore he who is poor and prudent, when he sees that the judge has been bought, shall keep silent at that time, for it is an evil time. Or certainly it is to be understood thus: What use is it now, when your captivity is near, to enumerate your sins, when there is no longer any remedy and a hostile army surrounds the walls of your cities?

When therefore a churchman, prudent and understanding, comes to know that there are many impieties in that which is called the house of God, and not only many but also strong, and such as can oppress righteousness, and that the madness of the teachers has gone so far that they take a price in judgment and do everything for gifts, and also shun the poor in the gates and disdain to hear them, let him be silent at that time, lest he give what is holy to dogs and cast pearls before swine, who would turn and trample them; and let him imitate Jeremiah, who says: I sat alone, because I was filled with bitterness. And that in the psalms: I am alone until I pass over.

5:14.t: Seek good and not evil, that you may live, and the Lord God of hosts will be with you, as you have said: Hate evil and love good, and establish judgment in the gates, if perhaps the Lord God of hosts may have mercy on the remnant of Joseph. LXX: Seek good and not evil, that you may live; and so the Lord God Almighty will be with you, as you have said: We have hated evil things and loved good things; and render judgment in the gates, that the Lord God may have mercy on those who are left of Joseph. You say that God is with you because you are sons of Abraham; hear what follows: If you are sons of Abraham, do the works of your father. What are the works of your father Abraham? Love good and not evil. It is a great sin not only to do evil but also to love it. […]

All these things can also be fitted to the heretics, so that, abandoning the error which they have invented, they may return to the Church, and hate their former dogmas, and love the truth of the Lord in the Church, and exercise true judgment in the gates of vices and virtues, leaving the former and passing over to the latter; and that those who have been able to escape from the jaws of the devil may hope for mercy. But according to the LXX, with the order changed, the reading of the present section can be rendered more plainly thus: As you have said, We have hated evil things and loved good things, so seek good and not evil, that you may live; […]

Seek good and not evil, that you may live, and so it will be the Lord God the Almighty with you; in the manner that you said, We have hated evil and loved good, and establish judgment in the gates, so that the Lord God the Almighty may have mercy on the remnant of Joseph. Therefore, in the manner you have spoken, he says, seek good and not evil, so that you may gain well-being by living and being saved, and the Lord God, who has authority over all, may be with you. And establish judgment in the gates, that is, become upright judges; not recording an unjust vote against the weaker; not misrepresenting the power of the just; nor indeed striking the heads of the poor; […]

It was the old custom that the elders should sit at the gate to make out by judicial trial the quarrels of persons at strife, in order that they should never enter the city at variance and should dwell there in harmony. And hence the Lord says by the prophet, "Establish judgment at the gate."
5:14.s: MORALS ON THE BOOK OF JOB 4:21.32

5:15.t: Nor is it enough to seek good and not to seek evil, unless you have ἐπιείκησιν (equity) in both, so that first you hate evil and then love good. He hates evil who is not only not overcome by pleasure, but hates the works of pleasure; and he loves good who does what is good not unwillingly, nor from necessity or fear of the laws, but because it is good, so that he has as the reward of his good work his own conscience and the love which he bears toward the good. Hence the Apostle too says: God loves, he says, a cheerful giver. For not every almsgiving pleases God, but only that which is offered with cheerfulness. And when you have hated evil and loved good, establish judgment in the gates, of which it was spoken above, so that, iniquity being driven out, truth may return. […]
And again it signifies Ephraim, that is, the ten tribes. For as I have already said before, since Ephraim came from Joseph, for this reason he is also signified by his father's name.

5:16.t: All these things can be referred to the heretics, so that, because they would not do this and that which is just, there may be wailing in all their streets. Wide indeed and spacious is the way that leads to death, and each of the heretics and of the gentiles has his streets in their fables and fictions; to which it is fittingly added: And in all the places that are outside it shall be said: Woe, woe. For those who are in the Church will not hear woe, which is the last of punishments; but if perhaps they have sinned, a lamentation will be taken up over them. […]

Therefore thus says the Lord God of hosts, the Ruler: In all the streets there shall be wailing, and in all the places that are outside it shall be said: Woe, woe. And they shall call the farmer to mourning, and to wailing those who know how to wail. And in all the vineyards there shall be wailing, for I will pass through the midst of you, says the Lord. LXX: Therefore thus says the Lord God Almighty: In all the streets wailing, and in all the ways it shall be said: Woe, woe. The farmer shall be called to mourning, and to wailing those who know lamentation, and in all the ways wailing, for I will pass through the midst of you, says the Lord. I commanded you to seek good and not evil, that you might live, and that the Lord might be with you. […]

5:17.t: And in all the vineyards there shall be wailing, for their vineyards are the vineyards of Sodom. And instead of the wine of gladness, which gladdens the heart of man, they have brought forth the wine of dragons and the incurable fury of asps. And they will suffer all these things, because the Lord will pass through their midst, so as not to dwell among them, nor to say: I will dwell in them, and walk among them, and: Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age.

5:18.t: But no one doubts that all our writers understand the day of darkness as the day of judgment, of which Zephaniah also writes: Near is the great day of the Lord, it is near and exceedingly swift: the voice of the day of the Lord is bitter and hard. And Isaiah: Behold, the incurable day of the Lord is coming, of fury and wrath, to make the whole world a desert, and to destroy the sinners out of it. And at the same time the confidence of the proud is shaken off, who, in order to appear just before men, are accustomed to await the day of judgment and to say: Would that the Lord might come, would that it were granted us to be dissolved and to be with Christ, imitating the Pharisee who spoke in the Gospel: God, I thank you that I am not like other men, robbers, unjust, adulterers, or […]

Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord: to what end is it for you? That day of the Lord is darkness and not light; as if a man should flee from the face of a lion, and a bear should meet him, and he should enter the house and lean with his hand upon the wall, and a snake should bite him. Is not the day of the Lord darkness and not light? And gloom and no brightness in it? LXX: Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord: to what end is this day of the Lord for you? And it is darkness and not light. As if a man should flee from the face of a lion, and a bear should fall upon him, and he should go into the house and lean with his hands upon the wall, and a snake should bite him. Is not the day of the Lord darkness and not light? And gloom, and it has no brightness. […]

Yet here a question arises: why do the saints desire the day of the Lord, when the prophet says, “Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord” (Amos 5:18)? For we know that the day of the Lord is the condemnation of the wicked, as we have already said. And what need was there for the prophet to say, “Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord,” when no wicked person is found who either desires his own death or the day of the Lord, since he fears being condemned in it? And because what the prophet said is true, we must investigate what it signifies. Indeed, the condemnation of the wicked is their sins: whoever therefore desires to go to bed with a prostitute, desires his own condemnation; whoever desires to get drunk, desires his own condemnation; […]

5:19.t: By these names there seem to me to be signified either various punishments or the devil himself, who is rightly called both lion and bear and snake. And when we think that we hear Isaiah saying: Go, my people, into your chambers; shut the door, hide yourself for a little while until the wrath of the Lord passes, and that we are as it were in our own house, as it were resting in hell, then the snake will bite us, which in the present place is called Nahas, and in Job is called Leviathan, about whose nature and manifold terror we learn more fully in that book itself. But in the gloom and darkness, which are the opposites of brightness and light, the diversity of torments is set forth.

5:21.t: I have hated and cast away your festivals, and I will not take in the odour of your gatherings. And if you bring me your whole burnt offerings and your gifts, I will not accept them, and I will not regard the vows of your fatlings. LXX: I have held in hatred and rejected your festivals, nor will I smell in your assemblies. And if you offer me holocausts and sacrifices, I will not accept them, and I will not regard the saving offering of your presence. This is said properly against the tribe of Judah, and against those who had migrated from Israel to the ceremonies of God, and nevertheless did not depart from the high places, and worshipped idols, and polluted the sacrifices of God by the greatness of their sins. […]

The word would be especially fitting for those from Judah and Benjamin. For the tribes in Samaria to the worship of idols being wholly attached, they were found to be very slothful and greatly negligent of the laws given through Moses; but those in Jerusalem sacrificed on the high places to Baal and offered libations to the host of heaven, yet in addition to this they pretended to take care to show reverence for the law, and to be eager to fulfill both sacrifices and feasts. But that the Creator of all things has hated these things, he also made clear through the voice of Isaiah, saying, "Hear the word of the Lord, you rulers of Sodom; attend to the law of God, you people of Gomorrah. What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me, says the Lord? […]

The difference, however, between the two services is very great: for the Saviour of all offers as a priest to God the Father the confession of our faith, and the "torrent of the sweet spiritual savour:"—for "God is a Spirit: and they that worship Him must worship in spirit and in truth." But the bloody sacrifices which they offer are not well-pleasing to God. For He even said to them, "I have hated, and have rejected your festivals, and I will not smell at your solemn assemblies. Because even though you bring Me whole burnt offerings and sacrifices, I will not accept them, nor will I regard the salvation of your appearance. Take away from Me the sounding of your praises: nor will I hear the psalmody of your instruments." […]
5:21.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

5:23.t: And besides, before His coming He refused the sacrifices of the people, while they frequently offered them, when they sinned against Him, and thought He was to be appeased by sacrifices, but not by repentance. For thus He speaks: "Why dost thou bring to me frankincense from Saba, and cinnamon from a remote land? Your burnt-offerings are not acceptable, and your sacrifices are not sweet to me." And afterwards: "Gather your burnt-offerings, together with your sacrifices, and eat flesh. For I did not command you, when I brought you out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt-offerings and sacrifices." And He says by Isaiah: "To what purpose do ye bring me a multitude of sacrifices? saith the Lord. […]
5:23.s: Constitutions of the Holy Apostles Book 6

5:23.t: Take away from me the tumult of your songs, and the canticles of your lyre I will not hear. LXX: Remove from me the sound of your songs, and the psalm of your instruments I will not hear. The beautiful canticles of the Levites, with which they praised God, he calls a tumult and a confused sound, because praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner, and they had been accustomed to offer these same things to idols as well. The prayer of the Jews also, and the psalms which they sing in the synagogues, and the composed praise of the heretics, are a tumult to the Lord and, so to speak, the grunting of a swine and the braying of asses, to whose cries the works of Israel are rather compared. […]

5:24.t: And judgment shall be revealed as water, and justice as a mighty torrent. LXX: And judgment shall roll as water, and justice as an impassable torrent. As water, if it slides down a slope, lays bare what it had covered before and makes it lie open to the eyes of all, so the judgment and justice of God, which he once judged concerning his own people, will lie open to all and will be borne along like a most mighty torrent. Whatever it seizes, it drags with it, and it suffers nothing to withstand it. But according to the Seventy the judgment of the worst men rolls about like water, because it does not stand in one opinion but is carried about by every wind of doctrine, disapproving what it had approved, and thinking what it had praised before to be worth nothing. […]

And judgment shall roll down as water, and righteousness as an impassable torrent. The righteous verdict against them will be like an impassable torrent, that is, dragging away what falls into it and sparing nothing. For when God drives someone into destruction and troubles, who is the one who will save? Who is the one who will help and deliver from judgment? Or what way will there be, by which if one passed through, he might be outside of the evils? None at all. "For who will turn back the high hand?" And, "If he shuts a man in, who can open it?" according to what is written.

And it is no difficult thing to see, that the message of the Gospel preaching, being small at first, was soon to leap forth as it were unto great increase, inasmuch as God had foretold of it by the voice of Isaiah, "that the whole earth has been filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as the deep waters that cover the seas." For the preaching of salvation is everywhere poured forth like a sea, and its onward course is irresistible. And this too the God of all clearly told us by the voice of the prophet, "And judgment shall roll as the waters, and righteousness as an impassable flood." […]
5:24.s: Commentary on the Gospel of Luke

5:25.t: We ask how they offered victims and sacrifice in the desert not to God but to their king, whom they call Lucifer? From the time when they transformed the gold into the head of a calf, saying: These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, everything they did is shown to have been done not for God but for idols. And as for our reading that afterwards they offered certain things to the Lord, they did it not willingly but out of fear of punishment, and because of the slaughter of those who fell on account of the idols; but the Lord regards not the things that are offered but the will of those who offer. […]

Did you offer victims and sacrifice to me in the desert for forty years, house of Israel? And you carried the tabernacle of your Moloch and the image of your idols, the star of your god, which you made for yourselves. And I will make you migrate beyond Damascus, said the Lord: the God of hosts is his name. LXX: Did you offer victims and sacrificial beasts to me in the wilderness for forty years, house of Israel, and you took up the tabernacle of Melchom, and the star of your god Repham, their figures which you made for yourselves. And I will carry you over beyond Damascus, says the Lord: God Almighty is his name. […]

That we may understand it so, Stephen, the first martyr of the Gospel, worthy of his name, relates in the history of the apostles: And they made a calf in those days, and offered a victim to the image, and rejoiced in the works of their hands. But God turned, and gave them up to serve the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: Did you offer sacrificial beasts or victims to me for forty years in the desert, house of Israel? And you took up the tabernacle of Moloch, and the star of your god Rhepham, the figures which you made to worship them, and I will carry you over beyond Babylon. Nor must the first martyr be thought to have erred because, where it is written in the prophet, Beyond Damascus, he said, Beyond Babylon. […]

5:26.t: But whatever is said according to the letter against the people of the Jews, refer all of it to those who worship idols under the name of Christ, and who, inventing perverse dogmas for themselves, carry the tabernacle of their king the devil, and the image of their statues and idols. For they do not worship one idol, but according to the variety of their doctrine they adore different gods, and the star of their god. Since he is an angel of Satan, he transforms himself into an angel of light, and falls from heaven like lightning, and the antichrist imitates Christ. And he fittingly added: Which you made for yourselves. For they did not receive these things from God, but fashioned them out of their own mind.

5:27.t: Therefore the Lord will make them migrate beyond Damascus, so that they may not drink the blood of the Lord, but may pass over into Babylon and hear through the prophet: Babylon is a golden cup, making all the nations drunk. For Damascus, as we have often said, means drinking blood, or the blood of sackcloth, so that through repentance they may be called forth to drink the blood of the Lord.

6:1.t: Jesus' miracle was performed in the district of Samaria, to which country also belonged one of the lepers. Samaria, however, had revolted from Israel, carrying with it the disaffected nine tribes, which having been alienated by the prophet Ahijah, Jeroboam settled in Samaria. Besides, the Samaritans were always pleased with the mountains and the wells of their ancestors. Thus, in the Gospel of John, the woman of Samaria, when conversing with the Lord at the well, says, "No doubt yours are greater," and again, "Our fathers worshiped in this mountain, but you say that Jerusalem is the place where men ought to worship." […]

Now that Samaria is to be understood of the heresies is proved both in the prophet Hosea and in many other places, and especially by that testimony: Woe to those who despise Zion and who trust in the mountain of Samaria; they have gathered as a vintage the chiefs of the nations; for all heretics despise 'Sion' [Zion], which means 'watchtower' and is referred to the Church, and they trust in the mountain of Samaria, namely in the pride of perverse doctrines which they think sublime, and through these frauds of preaching they gather as a vintage and lay waste the chiefs of the nations, so that, by the marvel of their doctrines, they draw all the powerful among the Gentiles into heretical error.

Woe to you who are wealthy in Zion, and trust in the mountain of Samaria; you nobles, heads of the peoples, entering with pomp the house of Israel. LXX: Woe to those who despise Zion, and trust in the mountain of Samaria; they have gathered the vintage of the firstfruits of the nations, and have gone in for themselves. To Zion, as we said above, and to the mountain of Samaria, that is, to the two tribes, which were called Judah, and to the ten, which were called by the name of Israel, the prophet's word is directed; […]

6:2.t: All that we have said according to the truth of the history, let us now transfer, according to the LXX translators, to the cloud of allegory. House of Israel, you who have withdrawn from me, who trust in the mountain of Samaria, who have gathered the vintage of the firstfruits of the nations, pass over and see, and go on to the very many walls, for this is what Hamath Rabba means; and from there go gently down into the winepress of those who fall while drinking: for this is what Gath and the Philistines signify. And contemplate everything, and especially the best kingdoms, or the best cities out of all the kingdoms; and consider whether their borders are more than yours. […]

Pass over to Calneh, and see, and go from there to Hamath the great, and go down to Gath of the Philistines, and to all the best kingdoms of these, whether their border is wider than your border. You who are set apart for the evil day, and draw near to the throne of iniquity, who sleep on beds of ivory, and wanton on your couches, who eat the lamb from the flock, and calves from the midst of the herd, who sing to the sound of the psaltery: Like David they thought they had instruments of song, drinking wine in bowls, and they are anointed with the best ointment, and they suffered nothing over the breaking of Joseph. […]

6:3.t: Those to whom he had said above: House of Israel, pass over, all of you, and see, from what sort of vices they are bidden to pass over to better things, the following words describe: Who come to the evil day, preparing for themselves by their own vice an evil day; not that any day is evil, but that each one prepares evil for himself, according to what we read in Ecclesiastes: Do not say, The former days were better for me than these, for you do not ask about this in wisdom; for it is foolish to lay it on the times, since it is in our power to make for ourselves either a good day or an evil one. These draw near to and touch false sabbaths. […]

6:4.t: Look also, I pray you, at those who stretch themselves upon beds of ivory, whom the divine Amos fitly upbraids, who anoint themselves with the chief ointments, and chant to the sound of instruments of music, and attach themselves to transitory things as though they were stable, but have not grieved nor had compassion for the affliction of Joseph; though they ought to have been kind to those who had met with disaster before them, and by mercy have obtained mercy; as the fir-tree should howl, because the cedar had fallen, and be instructed by their neighbours' chastisement, and be led by others' ills to regulate their own lives, having the advantage of being saved by their predecessors' fate, instead of being themselves a warning to others.

Since therefore the Jews, separating themselves from worldly things, devoted not themselves to spiritual things, to temperance, and gentleness, and hearing the divine word, but did the very opposite, feasting, drinking, indulging in excess and luxury; on this account it is, that the prophet condemns them. For he says, "Woe to them that come to an evil day," and, in continuation, "that make a Sabbath of lies." He shows by that which follows how their Sabbath became unprofitable. How then did they make it unprofitable? By their working wickedness, living in luxury, drinking, and doing numberless other base and vile acts. And that this charge is true, hear what follows; […]
6:4.s: Four Discourses on the Rich Man and Lazarus, Discourse 1

6:4.t: And what follows, You who sleep upon beds of ivory, we can interpret thus: he who is an athlete of the Lord, and is trained for wrestling, and prepares himself against the adverse powers, sleeps on the bare ground, imitating Jacob; and he puts at his head the stone which the builders rejected, and which has become the head of the corner. But those who give themselves to delights and luxury, and do everything for the sake of the belly, sleep on beds made of the ivory of a dead animal, and cling to unclean bones; and because vices seem beautiful and delight with their present sheen, they rest on their couches and are weighed down by the heaviest sleep. […]

Though you are about to suffer this, you now sleep on beds of ivory and wanton on soft couches, so as to couple lust with sleep. You eat not to drive away hunger and to sustain the human body, but for delights and luxury, so that whatever is tender and fat in the flocks and in the herds you make ready for your gullet; for you the lust of the genitals and of the throat, and a paunch seething with food, are not enough unless you soothe your ears with the songs of pipes and psaltery and lyre, so that what David did for the worship of God, devising the orders of the Levites and the varieties of instruments, you turn to pleasure and luxury.

6:5.t: They also clap with their hands to the voice and sound of the instruments, so that all their works look for pleasure, and they do nothing except what they provide for the belly and for lust. Nor let the prudent reader at once object to us this, and how it is written: Let the rivers clap with their hands, and: All nations, clap your hands, and: Shout for joy to God our helper. For there they are said to clap not to the sound of instruments, but to have one accord in the praise of God. After the voice of the instruments he added: They thought them as things standing, and not as things fleeing. […]

This most beautiful sense, in which it is said: They thought them as things standing, and not as things fleeing, is not found in the Hebrew, but in its place is written: Like David they thought they had instruments of song. Hence it seems to me to have been added by the translators, who in the description of luxury brought forth a maxim of this kind against vices and pleasures, so that they did not translate what was written, but added from their own what seemed good to them, or rather changed it.

6:6.t: And you drink wine in bowls, not to sate thirst but to overwhelm the mind. And you are anointed, not with the purest oil to soothe the labours of the body, but with the most costly ointments. And while you abound in these delights, if you see any of the people perishing, you are moved by no pity over their slaughter, but you despise them as brute animals and as beasts perishing in their own gore. This same sense the prophet Ezekiel also sets down under the example of the shepherds: Who eat the milk of the sheep, and are clothed with the wool, and devour whatever is choicest, and do not heal the wounded, do not bind up the broken, do not seek the perishing.

And what follows, Who drink strained wine, can properly be referred to the heretics, who approve some Scriptures and reject others, wishing to drink strained wines, although in the holy Scriptures nothing is muddy and miry, but all is most pure, from the water above. These are anointed with the first ointments who, not having the perfumer's art, without any knowledge of the Scriptures, and of the traditions and teaching of the apostles, claim for themselves the dignity of the priesthood, and say that they are the anointed of the Lord, and contaminate the purest oil with the dregs of their own understanding. […]

And if I may speak of those who have undertaken the direction of souls, how many there are today who reveal their lack of the requisite qualities! Only with a feeling of pain can I speak of this subject at all -- how they melt down in the furnace of their covetousness the insults endured by Christ, the spittle, the scourging, the nails, the lance, the cross, his death itself, and squander them in the pursuit of shameful gain. The very price of the world's redemption is bundled into their purses; and only in this do they differ from Judas Iscariot, that he reckoned the total value of these things at a paltry sum of money, while they, with a more ravening greed, demand riches beyond counting. […]
6:6.s: Sermons on the Song of Songs, Sermon 10

6:7.t: Therefore now they shall migrate at the head of those who migrate, and the faction of the wanton shall be taken away. The Lord God has sworn by his soul; says the Lord God of hosts: I detest the pride of Jacob, and I hate his houses, and I will deliver up the city with its inhabitants. And if ten men remain in one house, they too shall die; and his kinsman shall take him up, and shall burn him, to carry the bones out of the house, and he shall say to the one who is in the inner rooms of the house: Is anyone still with you? And he will answer: It is the end; and he will say to him: Be silent, and do not remember the name of the Lord. LXX: Therefore now they shall be captives from the beginning of the mighty, and the neighing of horses shall be taken away from Ephraim; […]

We have drawn the slender lines of the history; now let us set our hand to the allegory. The princes of the heretics, who for the sake of their delights devoured my people and suffered nothing over the breaking of Joseph, will be the first to be led to punishment, and the neighing of the horse will be taken away from Ephraim, which in the holy Scriptures is taken in two ways: either for the pride and power of those who neigh, or for the greatness of lust. For pride and the conspiracy of the wicked, as there: Some in chariots, and some in horses, and: A horse is deceitful for safety. And the kings of Israel are commanded not to multiply horses for themselves. And in the book of Job the voice of the horse is compared to the blast of the trumpet. […]

6:8.t: The Lord has sworn by himself, or, as we read in the Hebrew, by his soul, according to what is written in Isaiah: Your new moons and sabbaths and feast days my soul hates, not that God has a soul, but that he speaks with human affections. Nor is it surprising if he is said to have a soul, since he testifies that he has the other members too, which are lower than the soul, feet and hands and belly, and the other limbs. But if those who deny that Christ had a human soul, and say instead that in the human body God was in place of the soul, should raise this against us, let them hear that in Christ the substance of a soul is shown, just as the members of his body also had substance. […]

And the Lord swears by himself, since he has no one greater by whom to swear, that he detests all the insolences of the heretics and hates all their regions. For whatever they say is an insult, and worthy of the hatred of God. And he swears that he will take away the city and their meeting-places with those who dwell in them, namely both the people and the teachers, and that, even if ten men remain — men who, had they been in Sodom and Gomorrah, the fire would by no means have come down upon those cities — all will die that death which leads to Tartarus, of which Ezekiel writes: The soul that sins, it shall die.

6:9.t: And the wrath of God raged against them to such a degree that, even if ten men remain in one house, they too die, and a kinsman, or a neighbour, burns the corpses of the dead to carry the bones out of his house, because, for the crowds of the dying, whole bodies cannot be carried out. And when the one who has grown weary of carrying them away asks the one who is in the inner rooms of the house whether any remain whom he should hand over to him, and he answers: It is the end, I no longer have anyone to hand over to you for burial; then, before he can swear that he has none, the one who had asked, who was outside and had learned that there were none, commands him and says: Be silent, and do not remember the name of the Lord. […]

6:10.t: Their bones are buried by their kinsmen and their household, of whom it is said: Let the dead bury their own dead. And he who is outside, and does not enter the house of the dead, but rather casts the dead out, commands the one who burns the dead, and dissolves them into ashes, and crushes their bones, to be silent and not to stain the most pure name of God with a dead mouth. For God says to the sinner: Why do you declare my justices, and take up my covenant through your mouth? Hence we too must take care that we do not, being dead, bury the dead, but rather that, living, we lead forth to life those who are dead. If we do not do this, we are commanded and told, Be silent, because we are judged unworthy of the name of God.

6:11.t: For behold, the Lord will command, and he will strike the greater house with ruins, and the lesser house with rents. Can horses run on rocks, or can there be ploughing with wild oxen? For you have turned judgment into bitterness, and the fruit of righteousness into wormwood. You who rejoice in nothing, who say: Did we not by our own strength take horns for ourselves? For behold, I will raise up against you, house of Israel, says the Lord God of hosts, a nation; and they will crush you from the entrance of Hamath to the torrent of the desert. LXX: Therefore behold, the Lord will command, and he will strike the great house with ruins, and the small house with rents. Will horses give chase on rocks, will they keep silent toward the females? […]

Some, according to anagogy, think that the great house and the lesser house signify the Jewish people and the Church gathered from the Gentiles. For they are called great because of the fathers, and the law, and the prophets; we lesser, because we were without the covenant and the commandments of God, of whom we also read in the Song of Songs: My sister is little, and she has no breasts. This house, great and small, gathered into the one household of God, if it does not keep discipline and does not do the commandments of God, will be struck with ruins and rents. Whenever, therefore, the house of God, which is the Church, collapses and is torn, whether in persecutions or in heresies and schisms, it shows the hand of God striking; […]

6:12.t: The ruins and rents of these two houses he compares to horses and wild oxen: the former cannot run on rocks; the latter are so untamed that they do not take the yoke on their necks, and, being forest cattle, because of their wildness they refuse to cleave the earth with the ploughshare. But you, though horses and wild oxen cannot change their nature, have changed the nature of God, so as to make the sweet one bitter and to turn the fruit of his righteousness into wormwood, which is a most bitter herb.

Horses cannot give chase on rocks. The rock is Christ, who granted to his apostles that they too should be called rocks: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church. Whoever is on these rocks, the adverse powers, which are called horses, of which we spoke above, will not be able to pursue him, their courses being hindered and they falling on every single rock. Let us come also to the other comparison, according to our custom, discussing the edition of the LXX translators, lest, if we cling wholly to the Hebrew, we should seem to have mocked the diligence of the reader, and, by keeping silent about the common edition, to have set it out to no purpose. […]

6:13.t: Whence also we say that the holy men are just and that they are made pleasing to God after their sins not only through their merits but through the mercy of him to whom every creature is subject and stands in need of his mercy. Let heretics hear, who are lifted up by pride and say, "We have taken unto us horns by our own strength." Let them listen to what Moab heard said to him: "We have heard the pride of Moab, he is exceedingly proud. 'His haughtiness and his arrogance and his pride and the loftiness of his heart I know,' says the Lord, 'because his strength is not according to the loftiness thereof.' "

You who rejoice in nothing, either in idols and golden calves, which are nothing, as Esther says to the Lord: Do not hand over your sceptre to those who are not, or in nothingness and falsehood. You who think that by your own strength you took horns, and kings and power, with which to toss your enemies.

Those who do this rejoice in no good word, or in vain, as Symmachus translated, that is, ἀλόγως, and, lifted up in pride, they say: Did we not have horns by our own strength? Whereas, on the contrary, the just man glories in the Lord and says: In you we will toss our enemies with the horn. And in the same place: For I will not hope in my bow, and my sword will not save me. Hence also in Exodus, according to the Hebrew and the edition of Aquila, we read: And Moses did not know that the appearance of his face was horned, he who could truly say: In you I toss my enemies with the horn. […]

6:14.t: Because, therefore, you have done these things, behold, I will raise up against you, O great house and lesser house, which are to be struck with ruins and rents; that is, O house of Israel and all the twelve tribes, the most savage nation of the Assyrians and Chaldeans, to crush and overthrow you from beginning to end, from head to tail; from the borders of your land which look toward the sun, to the torrent of the desert, or of the west, as the LXX translated, that is, from Hamath to Rhinocorura, between which and Pelusium the stream of the Nile, or the torrent coming from the wilderness, enters the sea. We said above that Hamath is Epiphania, which took its name from Antiochus, whose surname was Ἐπιφανὴς (Epiphanes). […]

Because of these great sins and the utmost pride, which speaks iniquity against God and sets its mouth on high, the Lord God Almighty says that he will raise up a most savage nation, to crush and grind them down, or rather to forbid them to enter into Hamath, and as far as the torrent of the west. Hamath means wall, or walled. They were therefore forbidden by this most savage nation, to which the punishments had been entrusted, to flee for refuge to the fortified city, which is the heavenly Jerusalem, lest they enter and be saved; after the manner of that section which we read in Genesis, where God placed the Cherubim and the flaming sword which turns to guard the way of the tree of life, so that he who had been cast out of paradise might by no means enter there unworthy. […]

7:1.t: These things the Lord God showed me: and behold, the maker of the locust at the beginning of the shoots of the late rain, and behold, the late one, afterwards the king's shearer. And it came to pass, when it had finished eating the grass of the land, I said: O Lord God, be merciful, I beseech you; who will raise up Jacob, for he is very small? The Lord had pity over this: It shall not be, said the Lord. LXX: Thus the Lord showed me: And behold, a brood of locusts was coming in the morning; and behold, one cankerworm, Gog the king. And it will be, if it has finished devouring the hay of the land, and I said: O Lord God, be merciful; who will raise up Jacob, since he is small? Repent, O Lord, over this; and this shall not be, says the Lord. […]

The LXX translators seem to me to have understood the Hebrew word gozi, which means shearer or shearing, as Gog, taking the letter zai for uau, and to have compared the countless multitude of the cankerworm to Gog, a most savage nation, which is described as about to lay waste the land of Judea. But what Aquila meant to say with Behold, the late one after the king of Gaza, since Gaza is called Aza in the Hebrew word, I do not well understand, unless perhaps he set down the very word gozi, and it was gradually corrupted by error into Gaza. Let us speak also spiritually: those who after works of righteousness — of which it is said in the prophet: Sow for yourselves in righteousness, and break up fresh ground for yourselves; […]

7:2.t: And it came to pass, when the cankerworm that had come after the locust had finished eating the grass of the land, and the prophet understood what he was seeing, he turns to prayer and says: O Lord God, be merciful, I beseech you. I do not wish my words to be fulfilled in the overthrow of my people; I do not wish to have been chosen from the number of the shepherds for this, that I should announce the ruin of the ten tribes. For who will be able to raise up Jacob, except you alone? When you strike him down, there is no one to raise him up. Jacob is very small, and destroyed by the frequent incursions of enemies.

And when it has consumed the hay and the stubble of our land, whoever are saints among the people will pray for pardon and will say: O Lord God, be merciful. For who else will be able to raise up Jacob? Which of the physicians can heal the αἱμοῤῥοῦσαν (the woman with the issue of blood), except you alone, at the touch of whose fringe health at once returns? For Jacob is very small, or of small number, because no traces of virtues, or only a few, have remained in them.

7:3.t: And as he prayed and poured out the tears of the inner man, the Lord had pity over this and answered: I will not destroy the whole race of Israel; a remnant will be saved. Or certainly it is to be taken thus: he beheld two things to come together, first the locust, then the cankerworm. For both he entreated the Lord, and he is heard in one only, so that the cankerworm should not lay everything waste to utter destruction; but the locust, flying about, devours some things and leaves others untouched.

Repent, O Lord, over this which you threatened that you would do to your people. But the repenting of God in the Scriptures we ought to understand in the same way as his sleep and his anger: not that God repents or changes his sentence, he who speaks through the prophet: I am God, and I do not change, and to whom we say: But you are the selfsame, and your years will not fail; but that, when we are converted to better things, he too repents of his sentence, so that he neither pays the just man the rewards he promised, if he turns aside to iniquity, nor the sinner the punishments he threatened, if he is converted to salvation. […]

7:4.t: These things the Lord God showed me, and behold, the Lord God was calling judgment to fire; and it devoured the great deep and ate up a part as well. And I said: O Lord God, be still, I beseech you; who will raise up Jacob, for he is very small? The Lord had pity over this: But this too shall not be, said the Lord God. LXX: Thus the Lord God showed me, and behold, the Lord God called judgment in fire, and it devoured the great deep, and ate up a part; and I said: O Lord God, cease; who will raise up Jacob, since he is very small? Repent, O Lord, over this; and this shall not come to be, says the Lord God. […]

But since, once and for all, following the prophet Hosea and the psalmist, who says: The sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow, turned back in the day of battle, we have referred the ten tribes, which were called Israel, to the person of the heretics, and the two, over which Judah presided, to the Church and the sinners of the Church, who confess indeed the right faith, but because of the filth of their vices need flames to purge them; therefore the Lord now shows that he calls judgment to fire, so that the fire may prove of what sort each one's work is, and that may be fulfilled which is written: Walk in the light of your fire, and in the flame which you have kindled. […]

7:5.t: And when the prophet had seen this, he said to the Lord, not as above: Be merciful, I beseech you, but: Be still, or cease, so that by his prayers he might obtain that he whom he had already seen begin should cease, especially since there is no other who can raise up Jacob, fallen and very small and humbled, except the Lord, who is able to bring back into the land of Judah those taken captive and carried off into Chaldea.

And when we have all been in sin, and have lain prostrate before the truth of the sentence, the Lord will have mercy on us, and because we are very small, he will raise us up at the time of the resurrection, or he will raise up through virtues us who lay in vices; the Lord promising this and saying: But this too shall not be. And he said well: But this too, because above he had already said: This shall not be. Not, indeed, to the end will he be angry, nor for ever will he threaten. He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our iniquities. As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our iniquities from us. As a father has pity on his sons, so the Lord has had pity on those who fear him.

7:7.t: These things the Lord showed me: And behold, the Lord standing upon a plastered wall, and in his hand a mason's trowel. And the Lord said to me: What do you see, Amos? And I said: A mason's trowel. And the Lord said: Behold, I will set a trowel in the midst of my people Israel. I will not again overlay it, and the high places of the idol shall be demolished, and the sanctuaries of Israel shall be made desolate; and I will rise up against the house of Jeroboam with the sword. LXX: Thus the Lord showed me: And behold, a man was standing upon a wall of adamant, and in his hand adamant. And the Lord said to me: What do you see, Amos? And I said: Adamant. And the Lord said to me: Behold, I will cast adamant into the midst of my people Israel. […]

We have said as best we could what has been handed down to us by the Hebrews according to the truth of the history; let us pass to anagogy, setting down a few words from Xenocrates, who wrote on the natures of stones and gems: "Adamant is a stone of its own name, which in Latin we can call untamable, because it yields to no material, not even to iron. For if it is placed on an anvil and struck with a heavy blow of the hammer, the anvil and the hammer receive damage before the adamant is broken. And though fire tames all things and consumes all metals, it renders the adamant harder, so that the force of excessive heat does not blunt even the smallest corner of it. […]

7:8.t: We read in Ezekiel that the Lord threatens that, when storm and hail arise, he will by no means plaster or clothe the wall of Israel, but will let it be broken up by the rains. Hence now too he of whom it is written, He shall be called the builder of the wall, himself the cornerstone and the builder of the house, says that he will lay down the trowel in the midst of his people Israel, and make it cease and lie idle, so that he will by no means again overlay it, and clothe and protect it with his help.

The Lord therefore sets an adamant of this kind in the midst of his people Israel, and no longer passes him by, nor does he leave off, so that the altars, which deserve laughter and derision, are scattered, and he strikes with the sword and overthrows all the mysteries of the heretics and the house of Jeroboam, who first divided the people of God.

7:9.t: And when the Lord, the trowel ceasing, has withdrawn his protection and, so to speak, the clothing of the wall, then the high places of the idols, which in Hebrew are called bamoth, will be demolished, and the sanctuaries of the ten tribes will be made desolate, so that Dan and Bethel are destroyed, in which the golden calves were worshipped.

7:10.t: And Amaziah the priest of Bethel sent to Jeroboam king of Israel, saying: Amos has rebelled against you in the midst of the house of Israel. The land will not be able to bear all his words. For thus says Amos: Jeroboam shall die by the sword, and Israel shall go captive out of his land. And Amaziah said to Amos: You who see, go, flee into the land of Judah, and eat bread there, and there you shall prophesy; and in Bethel you shall not again prophesy any more, because it is the sanctuary of the king and it is the house of the kingdom. LXX: And Amaziah sent the priests of Bethel to Jeroboam king of Israel, saying: Amos is making gatherings against you in the midst of the house of Israel; the land will not be able to bear all his words. […]

All that we have interpreted concerning Amaziah, and Jeroboam, and Israel, and Amos must be referred τροπολογικῶς (tropologically) to the heretics, whose priest Amaziah is accustomed at times to send to Jeroboam, the heretical king and patron of heretics, and to accuse holy men and heralds of the faith before him, and to order the teachers not to preach in Israel, lest they act against the king's will, because Bethel, that is, the house of God, and the false Church is the sanctuary of the king and the house of the kingdom. For they are accustomed to say: The emperor is in communion with us; and if anyone resists them, they at once bring the slanderous charge: So you act against the emperor? You despise the commands of the Augustus? […]

7:11.t: For thus, he says, says Amos. You are wrong, slanderer. For in all his words the prophet does not speak as though from himself, but always sets at the head: Thus says the Lord. Therefore he makes out that the prophet Amos said what the Lord spoke, so as to provoke the king the more to vengeance. What are the things that Amos says? Jeroboam shall die by the sword. In this too you lie: for he did not say: He shall die; for if he had said this, it would seem that he did not admit repentance; but he said that the Lord will rise up against the house of Jeroboam with the sword, threatening punishment, not inflicting it. Nor does he say: Jeroboam shall die by the sword, but: I will rise up against the house of Jeroboam with the sword. […]

7:12.t: Moreover Jeroboam, despising the utterly empty messages of Amaziah, would give no answer to what he had sent him; whereupon Amaziah takes upon himself the authority of the priestly eminence, and speaks to Amos: You who see, go, flee into the land of Judah. The prophets, as we have often said, were formerly called seers, because they beheld with the eyes of the heart the things they said were to come. The prudent reader may ask why he calls him a seer, and by the prophetic name, the man whom he compels to leave the land of Israel. To him the answer must be either that he says it in mockery, κατὰ ἀντίφρασιν (by antiphrasis), since everything Amos says is a lie, or that he saw there were many among the people who listened to him gladly; […]

7:14.t: I have read indeed: I was a goatherd, plucking mulberries, and I think the prophet signified to us that he himself, a sinner, was converted from a flock of sinners; although it fits that the future prophet of the Gentiles should seem to have sought fruit among brambles, to have dug out food from brambles, as one who would place the discolored and fetid flocks of the Gentiles, the peoples of the nations, in the pastures of his writings, so that they might grow fat with spiritual refreshment, while he himself would milk spiritual milk from the converted sinner.

Amos also said, "I was no prophet, nor the son of a prophet, but only a herdsman, a gatherer of sycamore fruit. And God took me." But he did not say this to exalt himself, but to stop their mouths that suspected him as no prophet, and to show that he is no deceiver, nor says of his own mind the things which he says.

And Amos answered, and said to Amaziah: I am not a prophet, and I am not the son of a prophet, but I am a shepherd plucking sycamores. And the Lord took me when I was following the flock, and said to me: Go, prophesy to my people Israel. And now hear the word of the Lord: You say: You shall not prophesy over Israel, and you shall not drip upon the house of the idol. Therefore thus said the Lord: Your wife shall commit fornication in the city, and your sons and your daughters shall fall by the sword, and your ground shall be measured with the line, and you shall die in a polluted land, and Israel shall go captive out of his land. LXX: And Amos answered, and said to Amaziah: I was not a prophet, nor the son of a prophet, but a herder plucking sycamines. […]

How good it is to raise up eyes of faith to the power of this worker, the Holy Spirit, and to look here and there at our ancestors in the Old and New Testaments. With the eyes of my faith open, I gaze on David, on Amos, on Daniel, on Peter, on Paul, on Matthew—and I am filled with a desire to behold the nature of this worker, the Holy Spirit. But I fall short. The Spirit filled a boy who played upon the harp, and made him a psalmist; on a shepherd and herdsman who pruned sycamore trees, and made him a prophet; on a child given to abstinence, and made him a judge of his elders; on a fisherman, and made him a preacher; on one who persecuted the church, and made him the teacher of the Gentiles; on a tax collector, and made him an Evangelist. What a skilled worker this Spirit is! […]

If the spirit of prophecy had always been present to the prophets, the prophet Amos when asked would never have said, "I am no prophet"; he even adds, "neither a prophet's son, but I am a herdsman and a gatherer of sycamore fruit." How then was he no prophet who foretold so many true things concerning the future? Or in what way was he a prophet if he at the time disowned the truth concerning himself? At the moment that he was called in question, he felt that the spirit of prophecy was not with him. He bore true testimony concerning himself in saying, "I am not a prophet." Yet he added afterward, "Now therefore hear the word of the Lord. […]
7:14.s: MORALS ON THE BOOK OF JOB 1:2.89

7:16.t: Since, therefore, he says, when the Lord commands me to speak, you, Amaziah, say to me: You shall not prophesy over Israel, and you shall not drip upon the house of the idol, hear what the Lord threatens against you. For house of the idol, in the Hebrew is written beth isaac, that is, house of laughter, for Isaac means laughter; which the LXX translated house of Jacob, understanding one name in place of another, and not the thing. Again, where we have put: And you shall not drip, Symmachus translated: you shall not rebuke. Now that the prophets drip is an idiom of the Scriptures, because they do not bring on the whole wrath of God at once, but announce it in small drops by their threatening.

According to tropology, Amaziah the priest means strong and rigid, because, rebellious and fierce, he forbids the churchman and true prophet to bring forth the words and the teaching of God, and prohibits him from correcting the erring people. His wife, the false Church, will lie open to the fornication of all, and his sons and daughters, whom he wickedly begot in error, will be struck by the Lord's sword; his ground too and all his possession will be the portion of demons, and he himself will die in a polluted land, which does not have God as its inhabitant but is contaminated by the many errors of a depraved religion; […]

7:17.t: Because, therefore, you said to me: You shall not prophesy, your wife shall commit fornication in the city; which Symmachus translated better, πορνευθήσεται, not that she herself will commit fornication, but that, in the passive voice, violated by others, she will suffer fornication. And it is a great grief and an incredible disgrace when a husband, in the middle of the city, with everyone present, cannot prevent the outrage done to his wife. Your sons also, he says, and your daughters shall fall by the sword. The grief over a violated daughter is not so great as over a defiled wife, nor the grief over a slain wife so great as over slaughtered children. For a husband would more willingly have his wife killed than defiled. […]

8:1.t: These things the Lord God showed me: And behold, a hook for fruit, and he said: What do you see, Amos? And I said: A hook for fruit. And the Lord said to me: The end has come upon my people Israel; I will not again pass him by any more, and the hinges of the temple shall creak in that day, says the Lord God; many shall die, in every place silence shall be cast. LXX: Thus the Lord God showed me: And behold, a fowler's vessel. And he said: What do you see, Amos? And I said: A fowler's vessel. And the Lord said to me: The end has come upon my people Israel; I will not again pass him by any more; and the ceilings of the temple shall howl in that day, says the Lord God. Many will be falling: in every place I will cast silence. […]

But if we choose to read a fowler's vessel instead of a hook for fruit, this must be said: that as a fowler, with birdlime or nets, draws down to the earth birds that fly through the air and range on high, so the Lord, through Sennacherib or Nebuchadnezzar, whom we now understand as the fowlers, seized, bound, carried away and killed his people, who were formerly free and lofty through their observance of the law. For not unjustly are nets spread for birds. And this is to be referred not only to the time of the Babylonian captivity, but also to the coming of the Lord the Savior, when they said: Away with such a one from the earth; crucify him, crucify him; and they lost the wings of the dove. And the end came upon them, and the final captivity, and God spared them no longer.

8:2.t: And that we may know that this is what we say, God himself explains what the vision he had shown the prophet signifies: The end has come upon my people Israel. And what follows: I will not again pass him by any more, signifies this: that he will no longer pass over the iniquities of his people, nor neglect them, nor allow their crimes to pass unpunished.

8:3.t: And lest he seem to speak only of the ten tribes, he added: The hinges of the temple shall creak, or the ceilings, in that day, says the Lord. This, however, is to be taken ὑπερβολικῶς (hyperbolically): so heavy a weight of evils will press down that even the very hinges of the gates and the lofty ceilings will howl and feel an incredible devastation, when many will die and, the inhabitants being captured or killed, silence will be cast in every place.

And the hinges of the temple howled, or the ceilings of the temple, collapsing upon the slain people. And in every place silence has been cast, the Jews having Moses and the prophets, but not having the Word of God; reading the letter and losing the spirit, when their table was made into a snare, and into a recompense, and into a ruin; and their eyes were darkened, so that they should not see; and their ears were stopped, so that they should not hear; and their back was bowed down, so that they should not look up to heaven, but, with that woman of the Gospel who had a spirit of infirmity, should always be bent toward the earth. […]

8:4.t: Hear this, you who crush the poor and make the needy of the land fail, saying: When will the month pass, and we shall sell our wares, and the sabbath, and we shall open the grain, that we may diminish the measure and increase the shekel; and put in deceitful balances, that we may possess the needy for silver, and the poor for shoes, and sell the refuse of the grain. LXX: Hear these things, you who crush the poor in the morning, and oppress the needy from the land, who say: When will the month pass by, and we shall trade; and the sabbaths, and we shall open the granary, to make the measure smaller and the weight greater; and let us make an unjust balance, that we may possess the poor for money, and the needy for shoes, and trade in every sale. […]

And this indeed we sometimes see done also by perverse teachers and rulers, who without the fear of God lord it over the clergy, of whom Jeremiah speaks: Their clergy will not profit them; who think that gain is godliness, and, sitting in the temple as money-changers, set out doves, not in cages but in chairs, as though they were teachers, selling the gifts of the Holy Spirit; who make the measure smaller and greater, so that to the poor they speak either little or nothing, but to the rich, and to those from whom they pursue gain, they speak in the manner of public orators at very great length. And for money they crush and trample the heads of the poor, and thrust into greedy throats, not the grain of the Lord, which strengthens the heart of man, but refuse and the vilest dust; […]

8:5.t: You who wait for the Kalends, to trade and to heap interest upon interest, and for the sabbaths, to open the granaries and give out grain, meaning to receive more back, and who turn the solemn feasts of God to your own profit for the sake of shameful gain; who make the measure smaller in selling goods, and the weights greater in receiving them, and the balance unjust, so that you may possess the poor man's money, and hold men so cheap that you fulfill what I said of you above: Because you sold the righteous for silver, and the poor for shoes; you have leapt into such a frenzy for gain that you sell to the poor not grain, by eating which men's bodies are sustained, but the refuse and sweepings of the grain, mixing dust and chaff with the wheat.

8:7.t:
[Passage quoted, Amos viii. 7-12.]

THIS prophecy foretells the pride, insolence and rebellion of the Jews against our Saviour, and says that the Lord sware against the presumption of Jacob, that their insolence against Him should never be forgotten, and that their land and its inhabitants should undergo suffering and mourning, and that no more as before should they be punished a little while and then restored, but that this judgment should last for ever. For He says, "Complete destruction shall come upon them," meaning that wrath in the time of the Roman Empire would attack them, that a river should rise on them as on men who before were lifted up.

And then after this anger of God against them, their state, He says, will again "Come down like the river of Egypt." […]
8:7.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 10, Chapter 6

8:7.t: The Lord has sworn against the pride of Jacob: If I shall have forgotten all their works even to the end. Shall not the earth be moved over this, and every inhabitant of it mourn, and it rise up wholly like a river, and be cast out, and flow away like the brook of Egypt? LXX: The Lord has sworn against the pride of Jacob: If he will forget all your works to the end. And over these things shall not the earth be troubled, and every inhabitant of it mourn, and its consummation rise up like a stream, and go down like the river of Egypt? Scripture quite often records the Lord swearing. […]

And he swears that he will not forget their works even to the end; for the proud God resists, but gives grace to the humble; but that he holds in memory all the sins they have committed, and brings them even to the end and the time of judgment. Hence the penitent pray: Do not remember our former iniquities; especially since against the proud the earth itself is moved, or troubled, and mourns, not the tenant and the stranger, but its inhabitant; and its consummation rises up like a river, and goes down like the stream of Egypt, so that he who repents rises with the climbing river, but he who persists in his offenses goes down like the river of Egypt and, entering the sea, is swallowed up. […]

8:9.t:
And He next tells what will happen at the time of the saving Passion, "In that day," He says, saith the Lord, "the sun shall set at midday, and the light shall be darkened on the earth at daytime," and this was plainly fulfilled, when our Lord was lifted up, according to the Gospel:

"And there was darkness over all the earth from the sixth hour even to the ninth hour, and about the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani."
8:9.s: The Proof of the Gospel, Book 10, Chapter 6

8:9.t: For that lamp shone and they did not by it seek the Lord their God. And its light shone in the darkness and the darkness did not comprehend it. And the lamp was set up on the lamp-stand and those who were in the house did not see its light. And what then means this, that the lamp was set up on the lamp-stand? Clearly His being raised up upon the cross. And by this all the house was made dark over them. For when they crucified Him, the light was darkened from them, and shone amongst the Gentiles, because that from the time of the sixth hour (of the day) on which they crucified Him even unto the ninth hour there was darkness in all the land of Israel.
